books.title: Deep in the Ocean
books.art_why: Photographs suit real ocean animals, oceanographers, and modern science.

pages.text: Deep Underwater Imagine going deep in the ocean. What do you think you would see? Would it be dark or light? Would it be warm or cold? Would you find strange new animals and plants?
pages.brief: A deep underwater view shows dark blue water fading into lighter water above, with strange new animals and plants drifting and swimming, suggesting the imagined questions of whether the deep ocean is dark or light, warm or cold.

pages.text: Sunlight warms the surface and shallow parts of the ocean. Plants and animals that need sunlight and warm water live there. Other animals live in the cold, dark waters of the deep ocean.
pages.brief: Sunlight shines on the warm surface and shallow parts of the ocean, where plants and animals that need sunlight and warm water live, while other animals swim in the cold, dark waters of the deep ocean below.

pages.text: Ocean Zones.
pages.brief: A wide view of the ocean shows it divided into zones, layer by layer, from the surface down to deep water, with the upper ocean bright and the lower ocean dark, introducing the different ocean zones.

pages.text: Oceanographers Scientists who study the ocean are called oceanographers (oh-shuh-NOG-ruh-furs). They often live for months on a ship. Some study what a sea animal eats and where it lives.
pages.brief: Oceanographers working on a ship at sea live aboard for months, with open water around them, observing and studying sea animals; some study what a sea animal eats and where it lives in the ocean.

pages.text: Using Satellites for Tracking Satellites can help to track sea animals. Scientists tag some animals. A satellite can track the signal from the tag. The signal shows where the animal goes.
pages.brief: A scientist attaches a small tag to a sea animal below the surface while a satellite high above Earth tracks the signal from the tag, showing the route the tagged animal travels through the ocean.

pages.text: Counting the Sea Animals What animals live in the ocean? Where do they live? How many are there? Oceanographers studied and counted animals for ten years to find out. Their report is called the Census of Marine Life.
pages.brief: Oceanographers on a ship count and record many kinds of sea animals in the water below, working over ten years to find out what animals live in the ocean, where they live, and how many there are.

pages.text: The Census of Marine Life The census found living things everywhere! Marine species lived in the hottest and coldest places. Some lived in deep places without light or oxygen.
pages.brief: Many marine species are shown living everywhere, including in the hottest and coldest ocean places and in deep water without light or oxygen, filling even the most extreme parts of the ocean with living things.

pages.text: Living in Hot and Cold Water The very cold Deep Ocean Zone has hot volcanoes in it. The water temperature at a volcano can be 400°C (752°F). Some species of shrimp, crabs, worms, and bacteria live in this very hot water.
pages.brief: On the deep seafloor in the very cold Deep Ocean Zone, hot volcanoes send out superheated water at 400°C, and shrimp, crabs, worms, and bacteria live in the very hot water around the hot volcanoes.

pages.text: Huge groups of Arctic sea life were also found living in freezing water. Some species of squid, cod, and jellyfish live under thick sheets of solid ice.
pages.brief: Below thick sheets of solid ice in freezing Arctic water, huge groups of many kinds of sea life gather, including squid, cod, and jellyfish swimming together in the very cold, dark water beneath the ice.

pages.text: What Did We Learn? The marine census counted over 230,000 species. Over 6,000 new species had never been seen before! Some creatures were see-through. Some had warning lights that turned on and off. Others had long feelers instead of eyes.
pages.brief: A group of strange deep-sea creatures in the dark ocean shows the census discoveries: some are see-through, some have warning lights that turn on and off, and many others have long feelers instead of eyes.

pages.text: What else lives in the deep ocean? Scientists keep finding new species and new facts. They think that only one-fourth of all marine life has been counted. So there are many more surprises to come! Explore More To learn more about the Census of Marine Life, go to its website at www.coml.org. Each week, new discoveries are added to the marine census project map at www.comlmaps.org/census-on-google- earth. On the Internet, search terms such as deep sea species, blind lobster, or NASA oceanography.
pages.brief: Scientists exploring the deep ocean find new species and new facts, while many more unknown marine creatures remain unseen, suggesting that only one-fourth of marine life has been counted and more surprises are to come.

books.title: Pepper: The King of Spices
books.art_why: The book describes historical trade and old-world scenes that cannot be photographed today.

pages.text: Pepper: The King of Spices.
pages.brief: A decorative illustration of a pepper vine with green leaves and clusters of small round berries, alongside a few dried black peppercorns, on a soft, inviting background. The warm scene introduces pepper as the King of Spices.

pages.text: Introduction What is black and wrinkled like a tiny raisin? What has sent men sailing across the ocean and was once used as money? It’s pepper! You may have seen pepper in a shaker. You may have sprinkled it on your food. But do you know what it is? Do you know where it comes from? The pepper you eat comes from a dried- up berry called a peppercorn. If you have ever seen a peppercorn, you might have thought it was a pebble. But it is not. It is a berry that grows on a vine. People use the whole peppercorn or crush it into tiny pieces. They use it to add flavor to food. Plant parts that are used to flavor food are called spices.
pages.brief: A small dried peppercorn lies beside a tiny raisin, showing its black, wrinkled look. Nearby, a pepper shaker sprinkles crushed pepper onto food, while a green vine holds round berries that became the spice.

pages.text: Do You Know? Pepper can tickle the inside of your nose and make you sneeze. During a sneeze, air and other stuff can speed out of your nose at 161 km per hour (100 mph)! Pepper is a spice with a very strong flavor. People use it on meat and vegetables. You can mix it with other flavors to make plain foods taste better. Eating too much pepper can be bad for you. If you eat plain pepper, your tongue will feel like it is on fire. You might even feel hot inside. Some people can get sick if they eat too much pepper. Pepper is known as the King of Spices. This is because it is used more than any other spice in the world. As you read, you will find out that pepper was once even used as money!
pages.brief: A child sneezes after sniffing pepper, with a burst of air speeding from the nose. On a table nearby are meat, vegetables and a pepper shaker; a small crown rests beside them to show pepper as the King of Spices.

pages.text: How Pepper Grows The pepper plant grows as a long vine. The vines often wrap around a tree. Groups of round berries hang down from the vines. Each group can have thirty to seventy berries. When the berries dry out, they turn black and hard. They become wrinkled like a raisin. The dry berries are called peppercorns. Each peppercorn is smaller than a pea. Usually, people do not eat whole peppercorns. Instead, they use the type of pepper you see in a shaker. People use tools to grind peppercorns into tiny flakes. This makes pepper easier to eat.
pages.brief: A long pepper vine wraps around a tree trunk, with groups of thirty to seventy round berries hanging down. Some berries have dried black and wrinkled, smaller than a pea, and a hand tool grinds peppercorns into tiny flakes.

pages.text: Where Pepper Grows The pepper plant needs a lot of water to grow. This is why it is found in places that get a lot of summer rain. To dry out the berries, farmers also need a place with a warm, sunny autumn. By winter, the peppercorns can be used as a spice. One good place to grow pepper is the southwestern part of India. The weather is perfect for growing pepper vines. Farmers have grown pepper in India for thousands of years. The people of India used pepper to trade for things they wanted or needed.
pages.brief: Farmers in southwestern India tend pepper vines in a rainy summer landscape, while warm autumn sunlight helps dry the berries. Baskets of peppercorns sit nearby, ready to trade for things the farmers want or need.

pages.text: A Popular Spice Pepper has been used in many ways. Long ago, people used it to make meat taste better. Some people thought eating pepper could help them when they got sick. They also used it to make their homes smell good. One place where pepper is popular is Europe. Hundreds of years ago, it was very hard to get this spice there. It did not grow in Europe, but many people still wanted it. There was a very small supply of pepper but a big demand for it. This meant that people who had pepper could sell it for a high price. Peppercorns were in such demand that they were sometimes used as money. People might get paid in peppercorns. They could use their peppercorns to buy things they needed. They could even pay their rent with peppercorns!
pages.brief: In Europe hundreds of years ago, a merchant hands a small pile of peppercorns to a worker as payment. Only a little pepper is available, so it is costly; people use peppercorns to buy things and even pay rent.

pages.text: People could also trade peppercorns for other food. In Rome, a person could trade one pound of pepper for forty pounds of wheat! In Greece, pepper cost so much that most people could not afford to buy it. If a poor person had pepper, leaders might have thought it was stolen. Sometimes poor people were punished just for having pepper. It was clearly a spice only the rich could afford.
pages.brief: In a Roman market, a balance scale holds one pound of pepper against forty pounds of wheat. A wealthy buyer stands nearby, while a poor person is watched suspiciously for having pepper, showing that only the rich can afford it.

pages.text: A Long, Expensive Journey In the 1400s, people in Europe got a lot of their pepper from India. It grows in other places, too, but those places are even farther from Europe than India. To get pepper to Europe from so far away, people had to pay others to bring it to them. In the 1400s, it took over a year to get pepper from India to Europe. There were no planes, trains, or trucks back then. The peppercorns had to travel in carts or on the backs of animals, and sometimes by boat. As bags of peppercorns were moved from place to place, their price went up. Each worker had to be paid.
pages.brief: In the 1400s, bags of peppercorns travel from India toward Europe by cart, pack animal and boat. The long journey takes over a year, and each worker along the way must be paid, so the price rises.

pages.text: First, the pepper berries had to be picked in India. Farmers gathered them in large bags or baskets. Then they put them on big blankets to dry in the sunlight. All the farmers had to be paid. Workers loaded the peppercorns onto wagons, and the journey began. Strong animals pulled the wagons to a river. Bags of pepper were loaded onto boats. Then the boats took the pepper down a river to the shore. All the wagon and boat workers had to be paid. Now the pepper was ready to cross the ocean. It was loaded onto larger boats that sailed from India to Africa. The boat workers and the captains had to be paid.
pages.brief: Farmers in India pick pepper berries and gather them in large bags and baskets. Workers spread the berries on blankets to dry in sunlight, load them onto wagons pulled by strong animals, then onto boats heading downriver.

pages.text: When the pepper arrived in Africa, it had to move over land. A strong buffalo or camel carried it. The pepper was taken down the Nile River on a wide boat. The boat workers and the people who led the animals all had to be paid. The load of spice had to cross the sea between Africa and Europe. So it was put onto one last boat. It could be sent to Greece, France, or many other countries. All the boat workers had to be paid.
pages.brief: In Africa, a buffalo or camel carries bags of pepper over land. Workers load the bags onto a wide boat on the Nile River, then onto one last boat for the sea crossing to Europe, with every worker paid.

pages.text: When the boat reached Europe, the journey was almost complete. The pepper was carried over land by carts. All the drivers had to be paid. At last, it was sold at a high price. This helped pay everyone who worked to get it to Europe. Kings and queens in Europe paid their own explorers to find new ways to bring back spices and other riches. Explorers were able to sail from Europe all the way to India and back. This was cheaper than bringing it over land.
pages.brief: At a European port, carts carry bags of pepper over land to be sold at a high price. In the background, an explorer's sailing ship leaves for India, seeking a cheaper sea route for spices and other riches.

pages.text: Pepper Today Pepper is used around the world today. But it is much, much cheaper now. You can buy it in a store with just a few coins. Many places even give it away for free. Imagine how a king from 600 years ago would feel if he saw free pepper! Why is pepper cheaper today? Now there is enough supply to meet the demand. Also, people can ship peppercorns around the world in just a few hours. People use fast ships, trains, trucks, and even airplanes to quickly get pepper to those who want it.
pages.brief: A modern store shelf holds pepper for a few coins, and a free sample sits nearby. Outside, fast ships, trains, trucks and airplanes move peppercorns around the world, making pepper much cheaper than in the past.

pages.text: Thinking Critically Today, as in the 1400s, people use pepper more than any other spice. Do you think pepper will always be the King of Spices? The pepper that comes out of your shaker is just like the pepper from 2000 years ago. It tastes the same. It still grows in India and in rainy parts of the world. So the next time you grind pepper on your food, imagine you are a king or queen. Think of what you could have bought in the 1400s with a whole shaker full of the King of Spices. It was like sprinkling your food with little bits of gold!
pages.brief: A child grinds pepper from a shaker onto food, imagining a royal crown and peppercorns like little bits of gold. Behind, pepper vines grow in a rainy landscape, showing the spice is still the same as long ago.

books.title: Salt Rocks!
books.art_why: The book includes ancient mines, mummies and historical scenes, so drawing fits.

pages.text: Take It with a Grain of Salt If your friends told you to eat rocks, would you? Perhaps you would take what they say with a grain of salt. This means that you should not trust that everything you hear is true. When you eat salt, you actually are eating a rock. Well, it’s a mineral, to be more exact. It comes in little crystals. Hey, my name is Crystal, too! It may surprise you to learn just how important this little white mineral can be. Well, you’re about to read a whole book on it.
pages.brief: A curious child stands with two friends who offer a small rock to eat, one friend holding it out and the child hesitating. Beside them, clear white salt crystals sparkle in a little pile, and a girl named Crystal points at the crystals with a surprised, friendly smile.

pages.text: First of all, there is salt in your body right now. In fact, without salt you would die! People and animals need salt to live. Your body uses salt to make your muscles move and to help your blood flow. Salt also helps you make good use of the food you eat and controls the water inside you. It even keeps your heart beating. If you have too little salt in you, you may feel tired or dizzy. But putting too much salt inside you can make you sick. Over many years, too much salt can make your heart and other parts of your body weak.
pages.brief: A child runs with strong muscles, then pauses looking tired and dizzy. Inside the child, a heart beats and blood flows; animals nearby also look healthy. A second child sits slumped, showing how too much salt over many years can weaken the heart and body.

pages.text: Do You Know? The average American eats 15 lbs (6.8 kg) of salt per year —the weight of a heavy bowling ball. Many foods already have a lot of salt in them. But sometimes people add more salt for seasoning. Salt is not known as a spice because it does not come from a plant. But salt and spices both add flavor to food. Sodium is another word for salt. One little spoonful of salt has as much sodium as your body needs for a whole day. The label on a food or drink package tells you how much sodium it has. If there is a lot of salt, there will be a lot of sodium. A lot of people try to eat foods low in sodium. They know that too much of it can be harmful. You may have seen foods marked low in sodium.
pages.brief: A family eats salty foods at a table. Beside them, a heavy bowling ball rests next to a large pile of salt equal to a year's amount. A small spoon holds one day's sodium, and a food package sits nearby.

pages.text: Don’t Rub Salt in the Wound Salt can do much more than make food taste better. A common use is to keep food from spoiling. Long ago, there were no refrigerators or cans to keep food fresh. So people put salt on meat and soaked vegetables in salt water. It helped them preserve the food so they could eat it later. But be aware! Salt is not a magic tool. Once a food spoils, salt will not make it safe to eat again. Salt Sayings.
pages.brief: Long ago, before refrigerators and cans, people rub salt onto pieces of meat and soak vegetables in salt water. They work in a simple kitchen or outdoor food store, preserving food for later. A spoiled piece of food nearby shows that salt cannot make unsafe food safe again.

pages.text: Would you put salt in your milk? Probably not. People once tried to keep milk from going bad by adding salt to it. Yuck! This did not work very well. Fortunately, we have discovered many other uses for salt. Which of these are other ways people have used salt? • treat illness • put out fires • clean fish tanks • kill weeds • treat bites and stings • make glass • wash clothes • treat poison ivy • clean chimneys • make leather Answer: all of them!
pages.brief: A person pours salt into a glass of milk and grimaces at the taste. Around them, small scenes show salt used to treat a bee sting, put out a fire, clean a fish tank, kill weeds, wash clothes, make glass, and clean a chimney.

pages.text: Mummies and Fast Cars!
pages.brief: An ancient wrapped mummy stands upright beside a sleek, fast race car. The mummy's bandages are visible, and the race car gleams with speed, set together against a plain background that shows both the old and the new.

pages.text: Salt of the Earth Salt is a natural material called sodium chloride. It is found all over the world and comes in little, clear crystals called grains. In nature, large groups of salt grains stick together and form rocks. Rocks of salt are often white, like the salt you eat. But I bet you didn’t know that salt rocks can also be brown, orange, or even pink! Salt Sayings.
pages.brief: Close up, clear salt grains form little crystals, and larger groups of grains stick together into salt rocks. Several salt rocks sit in a row, showing white, brown, orange, and pink colors, resting on the ground where they are found in nature.

pages.text: Back to the Salt Mines Salt is found all over the world. It can be found in the sea and on the land. But it is hard to get the salt from these places. Much of the salt in the world is dissolved in ocean water. To get the salt out, people in the past heated large pots of salt water over fires. Others filled ponds with ocean water. The heat from the fire or the Sun made the water evaporate. The salt crystals stayed behind. Try This!
pages.brief: People in the past heat large pots of salty ocean water over a fire, and shallow ponds filled with ocean water sit under the hot Sun. Steam rises as the water evaporates, leaving white salt crystals behind in the pots and ponds.

pages.text: People do not get salt only from the oceans. There are a few places in the world where rocks of white salt lie right on the ground. You could pick one up, crush it, and sprinkle it right onto a bowl of popcorn. But these places are rare. Most salt on land is buried deep underground. When people found salt buried underground, they dug it out and used it. Where there was a lot of salt and it was deep, workers dug a mine. Salt Sayings.
pages.brief: A person crouches by rare white salt rocks lying on the ground, crushing one and sprinkling it onto a bowl of popcorn. Behind, workers dig deep underground to reach buried salt, and a mine opening leads down into the earth.

pages.text: People living in Germany hundreds of years ago built a salt mine inside their mountains. Men broke off large rocks of salt with strong tools. They used animals to haul it out to the villages. Giant wooden slides brought workers down into the mine and helped pull out the heavy salt rocks. Today, there is a huge salt bed beneath part of the United States and Canada. One of the biggest salt mines in the world is under the city of Detroit, Michigan. There are about fifty miles of underground roads made of salt! The salt mine is as deep as the height of a tall building.
pages.brief: Hundreds of years ago in Germany, men break large salt rocks with strong tools inside a mountain mine, while animals haul the salt out to villages and a giant wooden slide carries workers down. Today, a huge salt mine beneath Detroit has long underground roads made of salt.

pages.text: Are You Worth Your Salt? Salt was hard to get in most places two thousand years ago. It was very expensive and had to be kept locked up. Salt was so special that some people were paid with salt instead of money! Today, salt is very cheap and easy to find. Many places give it away for free. You see it on the table at most restaurants. Salt Sayings.
pages.brief: Two thousand years ago, salt is locked up because it is expensive, and workers receive handfuls of salt instead of money. In a modern restaurant, a salt shaker sits freely on a table, showing how cheap and easy salt is to find today.

pages.text: Salt makes it harder for water to freeze. So we put over half the salt that comes from mines onto icy roads and sidewalks. This helps keep cars from crashing and people from slipping. Imagine a visitor from two thousand years ago seeing a huge truck just dumping precious salt on a road! Did You Know? Be happy you live in a time when salt is easy to find. Your body needs salt to live—that’s crystal clear. You do not have to take that fact with a grain of salt.
pages.brief: A huge truck dumps salt onto an icy road and sidewalk while cars pass safely and people walk without slipping. An amazed visitor from two thousand years ago watches the precious salt being spread, and a child nearby looks happy and healthy.

books.title: Whales
books.art_why: Real whales, oceans, people and boats can be photographed.

pages.text: Types of Whales There are about 75 kinds of whales. Most whales fall into one of two groups. One group has teeth. They are called toothed whales. The other group does not have teeth. They are called baleen whales. Toothed whales, which include dolphins and porpoises, have jaws lined with sharp teeth. They eat fish, squid, and other sea life. Larger toothed whales even eat seals. The killer whale, or orca, is a well-known toothed whale. Orcas are called killer whales because they are very good at hunting other animals.
pages.brief: A killer whale swims through dark blue ocean water, its jaws open to show sharp teeth as it hunts. Nearby fish and a squid dart away. Another whale opens its mouth to show baleen instead of teeth, showing the two groups of whales.

pages.text: One of the strangest whales is the narwhal. It is a toothed whale. The male narwhal has a large tusk growing straight out of the front of its head. The tusk can be up to eight feet long. Baleen whales have a special material, called baleen, that hangs from their upper jaw. Baleen looks a little like a giant feather or comb. It filters small fish and very small sea life from the ocean. It seems strange that such large creatures eat such tiny food.
pages.brief: A male narwhal swims in cold ocean water, a long straight tusk pointing forward from its head. Beside it, a baleen whale opens its mouth to show comb-like baleen hanging from the upper jaw, filtering tiny fish and sea life.

pages.text: Baleen whales feed in different ways. Some feed by moving slowly through water. They swim with their mouths open. As they do, they trap small animals from the water that passes through the baleen filter. The trapped food is then swallowed. Other baleen whales swallow huge gulps of water. A single gulp could fill a couple of swimming pools. A whale then forces the water out of its mouth through the baleen filters. The whale swallows the food filtered out of the water. Most whales live in salt water. But a few live in freshwater rivers. Since water makes things buoyant, it helps support the weight of large whales. Where Whales Live.
pages.brief: A baleen whale swims slowly with its mouth open, water passing through baleen to trap small animals. Another baleen whale takes a huge gulp, its mouth stretched wide. In a freshwater river, a whale surfaces, supported by buoyant water.

pages.text: Gray whales move between summer feeding grounds in cold waters and warm seas where baby whales are born. Russia Alaska Canada Summer Range Main Route Alternate Route You can find saltwater whales in most of the world’s oceans. They range from the North Pole to the South Pole. Some whales migrate great distances. For example, some whales migrate thousands of miles to feed and reproduce. PACIFIC OCEAN United States Mexico Winter Range Freshwater whales can be found in certain rivers. Pink dolphins live in the Amazon River. They have been found more than 1,600 kilometers (1,000 miles) up the river. Pink Amazon River dolphin.
pages.brief: Gray whales swim from cold summer feeding grounds toward warm seas where babies are born. Other whales surface across ocean waters from the North Pole to the South Pole. In the Amazon River, a pink dolphin swims far upstream in freshwater.

pages.text: Characteristics of Whales Whales are mammals. They have lungs and must surface for air. Whales do not breathe through their mouths. Instead, they breathe through a blowhole on the top of their head. Whales have a constant body temperature. A whale’s body temperature is 99 degrees Fahrenheit. It is almost the same as a human’s. Female whales give birth to live young. They feed their young with milk from special glands. This milk is rich in fat. A large female whale can produce more than 600 liters (150 gallons) of milk a day.
pages.brief: A whale surfaces and breathes through a blowhole on top of its head, a mist of spray rising. Below, a female whale swims beside her calf as it nurses, showing milk from special glands. The scene shows a whale’s warm body and live young.

pages.text: Whales have a thick layer of fat called blubber. The blubber lies just beneath the skin. It can be up to 50 centimeters (20 in) thick. The layer of blubber keeps whales warm when they are in very cold water. Whales store food as fat or blubber. They use the blubber for energy when food is scarce. And since blubber is lighter than other parts of the whale’s body, it keeps the whale from sinking. Whales have two large flippers that are paddle-shaped. They also have a large fan-shaped tail. These parts help whales move through the water. They use their flippers to steer. They use their tail to push themselves through the water.
pages.brief: A whale swims in very cold water, a thick layer of blubber shown beneath its skin. Its two large paddle-shaped flippers steer while its wide fan-shaped tail pushes it forward. The blubber keeps it warm, stores energy and helps it float.

pages.text: The larger whales can make very loud sounds. A blue whale makes the loudest sound of any animal. Sound is measured in units called decibels. The sound of a blue whale can reach 150 decibels. In comparison, a jet engine is 110 decibels. So whales are very noisy creatures. A blue whale can be heard through the ocean for over 1,600 kilometers (1,000 miles). Some whales, such as dolphins, make a clicking sound. The sound bounces off objects and returns to the dolphin. Dolphins use the echoes of sound to locate objects in the water. Sperm whales also use this method when hunting for fish and squid in deep, dark water.
pages.brief: A blue whale opens its mouth in deep ocean, rings of sound spreading far through the water. Nearby, a dolphin clicks and listens as echoes bounce off objects. A sperm whale dives in dark water, using sound to hunt fish and squid.

pages.text: Whale Behavior Whales spend much of their time diving below the water. Whales store lots of oxygen in their blood and muscles. When a whale dives, its heart slows down. This means it uses up less oxygen. Some whales can stay under water for a little less than an hour. Other whales can stay under for over an hour. Deep-diving sperm whales can stay under for up to 80 minutes. Whales usually swim in groups called pods. A pod consists of male and female whales of many different ages. The young whales swim with their mothers. Some pods are smaller and consist only of family members. Others are large and can have over 100 members.
pages.brief: A sperm whale dives deep underwater, its heart slowed and oxygen stored in blood and muscles. Nearby, a pod of whales swims together, males, females and young of different ages. Some young whales stay close to their mothers in the group.

pages.text: Many whales migrate to warm tropical waters in the winter. They go there to have their babies. In the summer they migrate to polar regions. They go to polar waters because of the rich source of food found there. Whales often seem to cooperate with each other. One type of cooperation is bubble feeding. When whales bubble feed, they form a circle. They release bubbles from their blowholes. The bubbles make a curtain that traps small fish. Each whale takes a turn eating fish inside the curtain.
pages.brief: Whales swim toward warm tropical waters in winter, then toward food-rich polar seas in summer. In a circle, several whales release bubbles from their blowholes, forming a curtain that traps small fish. One whale moves inside the bubble curtain to eat.

pages.text: Threatened Whales For years, whales were hunted for their meat and blubber. The blubber was used for lamp oil. It was also used to make paint, soap, and cosmetics. As ways of hunting improved, more and more whales were killed. Many types of whales were hunted to near extinction. Pollution of the oceans is also threatening whales. Whales eat fish that have toxic chemicals in their bodies. As whales eat more and more of these fish, they become poisoned. Scientists also think that noise pollution is interfering with long-distance whale communication.
pages.brief: People on a whaling boat approach whales in the ocean, showing how whales were hunted for meat and blubber. In polluted water, a whale swims near fish carrying toxic chemicals. Underwater noise spreads through the sea, interfering with long-distance whale communication.

pages.text: Efforts have been made to protect whales. As a result, some types of whales are increasing in number. But whales reproduce slowly. So it will take hundreds of years to get whale populations back to safe levels. blowhole (n.) page 13 opening on the top of a whale’s head used for breathing pod (n.) page 20 a group of whales narwhal (n.) page 7 a type of toothed whale that has a long, straight tusk growing out of its head buoyant (adj.) page 10 able to float blubber (n.) page 15 a layer of fat found beneath the skin of whales extinction (n.) page 23 the process by which an entire group of animals or plants dies out baleen (n.) page 8 special material in the mouth of certain whales that filters food from ocean water decibel (n.) page 17 a unit of sound Glossary.
pages.brief: A female whale swims with her calf in clear ocean water, showing the slow reproduction of whales. Behind them, a small pod surfaces and dives, suggesting protected populations beginning to increase after many years of protection efforts.

books.title: Jenny Loves Yoga
books.art_why: Real children practicing yoga today can be photographed.

pages.text: Each morning Jenny begins her day by practicing yoga. Yoga is an exercise that helps Jenny to grow strong and flexible. To practice yoga, Jenny moves her body into different positions called poses. Jenny holds the poses while she breathes in and out slowly through her nose. Chair Pose.
pages.brief: Jenny begins her day practicing yoga, moving her body into different poses and holding them while she breathes in and out slowly through her nose. She is shown in a chair-like seated pose, building strength and flexibility.

pages.text: Getting started Jenny wakes up very early and puts on her yoga clothes. Loose or stretchy shorts and a T-shirt work well. She rolls out a rubber mat. The mat helps keep Jenny from slipping while she is moving from one pose to another.
pages.brief: Jenny wakes up very early and puts on loose, stretchy shorts and a T-shirt. She rolls out a rubber mat on the floor, then gets ready to move from one pose to another without slipping.

pages.text: Mountain Pose Jenny begins by standing very straight at the front of her mat. She places her palms together in front of her heart. She closes her eyes and listens to the sound of her breath. This pose is called Mountain Pose. Jenny stands very still for several minutes. She is practicing being as strong and quiet as a mountain.
pages.brief: Jenny stands very straight at the front of her mat. She places her palms together in front of her heart, closes her eyes, and listens to her breath. She stays still for several minutes, practicing being as strong and quiet as a mountain.

pages.text: Jenny has friends around the world who love yoga too. Like Jenny, they begin their day at dawn. As the sun rises, they practice the Sun Salutations. A salutation is a greeting, or a way of saying “hello.” The Sun Salutations are a series of poses linked together. With each breath, the person moves from one pose to the next. To begin his Sun Salutation, Nikhil breathes in through his nose. He reaches up, stretching his fingertips to the sky. This is the beginning of the Sun Salutations.
pages.brief: At dawn, as the sun rises, Nikhil begins the Sun Salutations. He breathes in through his nose and reaches up, stretching his fingertips toward the sky. Around the world, Jenny and her friends begin their own yoga practice at the same early hour.

pages.text: As he breathes out, Nikhil bends at his waist. He folds forward, reaching toward his toes. Then, breathing in, he lifts his chin. He walks his feet back as he lowers his body to the floor with his arms. Breathing in, he begins to straighten his arms. He lifts up his chest and head as he presses his hands into the ground. He leans his head back. This pose is named after a kind of snake called a cobra. A cobra snake lifts its head up and back to scare away an enemy. Nikhil makes sure to continue breathing while he holds the pose. Forward Fold Cobra Pose.
pages.brief: Nikhil breathes out and folds forward toward his toes. Breathing in, he walks his feet back, lowers his body with his arms, then presses his hands into the ground and lifts his chest and head, leaning back into a cobra-like pose while continuing to breathe.

pages.text: Then Nikhil pushes back into a pose called Downward Dog. This pose looks similar to the way a dog stretches after a nap. His hands and feet press into the floor as he begins to straighten his legs. After a few breaths he bends his knees and hops forward. Breathing out, Nikhil folds over his legs again. Breathing in, he lifts up his hands and chest to the sky. Breathing out, he lowers his arms back into Mountain Pose. Nikhil moves through five sets of the Sun Salutations. This series of poses warms up the muscles of the legs and the back. These poses also strengthen the arms. Downward Dog Pose.
pages.brief: Nikhil pushes back into a downward-dog pose with hands and feet pressing into the floor. After a few breaths, he bends his knees, hops forward, and moves through five sets of Sun Salutations, warming his legs and back and strengthening his arms before returning to Mountain Pose.

pages.text: Triangle Pose Jenny’s friend Kiko does Sun Salutations too. After Kiko has moved through her Sun Salutations, she is ready to do other yoga poses. She steps her feet apart and stretches out her arms. The rubber mat keeps her feet in place. Kiko begins to bend at the waist. She leans out over her leg and reaches down to touch the floor. Carefully, she turns her head to look up at the ceiling. Can you see why this pose has been named the Triangle Pose?
pages.brief: Kiko steps her feet apart on her rubber mat and stretches her arms out. She bends at the waist, leans over her leg, reaches down to touch the floor, and carefully turns her head to look up at the ceiling in a triangle-shaped pose.

pages.text: Tortoise Pose Kiko likes to do poses that remind her of her favorite animals. Can you see why this pose might remind people of a tortoise? Fish Pose Rabbit Pose Kiko enjoys practicing this pose, named after a big fish. The Rabbit Pose is a wonderful way to stretch the muscles of the neck.
pages.brief: Kiko practices yoga poses named after animals. She folds into a tortoise-like shape, moves into a fish pose, and then takes a rabbit pose that stretches the muscles of her neck. She enjoys poses that remind her of her favorite animals.

pages.text: Some yoga poses are named after things they resemble. Jenny’s friend Devan likes to practice the Boat Pose. He sits and holds the backs of his knees with his fingers. Devan leans back as he straightens his legs. He imagines he is a little boat floating on the surface of the water. Devan also loves to practice balancing poses. These poses help to strengthen the legs and feet. First, he stands on one leg and focuses his gaze on one spot on the floor or wall. As he leans forward, he lifts his other leg up and back. He holds his arms out like wings. He pretends he is floating like an airplane. Airplane Pose Boat Pose.
pages.brief: Devan sits in a boat pose, holding the backs of his knees with his fingers and leaning back as he straightens his legs, imagining he is a little boat on the water. Then he balances on one leg in an airplane pose, arms out like wings, pretending to float.

pages.text: Another balancing pose is called the Tree Pose. Again, Devan stands on one leg. He tries to make this leg feel as strong as the trunk of a tree. Slowly, he begins to lift his arms up to the sky. As he balances, he breathes calmly in and out through his nose. He imagines that his arms are branches and his fingers are the leaves. Tree Pose.
pages.brief: Devan stands on one leg in a tree pose. He lifts his arms up to the sky and breathes calmly in and out through his nose. He imagines his standing leg is a strong tree trunk, his arms are branches, and his fingers are leaves.

pages.text: Near the end of their yoga practice, Jenny and her friends practice inversions. An inversion is a pose in which the body is held upside down. It helps to prevent soreness in the muscles. Kiko’s favorite inversion is the shoulder stand. She lifts her legs up toward the ceiling. She bends her elbows and uses her hands to support her back. She holds the pose for a few minutes. Shoulder Stand Nikhil also likes to practice this simple inversion. He lies on the floor and lifts his legs. As he leans his legs against the wall, he reaches his hands out to the sides. An inversion.
pages.brief: Kiko holds a shoulder stand, lifting her legs toward the ceiling, bending her elbows, and using her hands to support her back. Nearby, Nikhil lies on the floor and lifts his legs, leaning them against a wall while reaching his hands out to the sides in a simple inversion.

pages.text: Jenny and her friends are almost finished with yoga practice. They will do the Lotus Pose. Devan gets into Lotus Pose. He crosses one leg over the other in the shape of a pretzel. He makes his back straight and tall. He rests his hands on top of his knees. He sits very still and closes his eyes. He listens to the sound of his breath. This helps Devan feel calm. Sitting in a Lotus Pose.
pages.brief: Devan sits in a lotus pose with one leg crossed over the other in the shape of a pretzel. His back is straight and tall, his hands rest on top of his knees, and he closes his eyes, sitting very still and listening to his breath to feel calm.

pages.text: Jenny uses a blanket to keep warm. Jenny always makes sure to finish her yoga practice with a rest. She lies down and covers her body with a blanket. She closes her eyes and completely relaxes her arms and legs. She stays in this pose for several minutes.
pages.brief: Jenny finishes her yoga practice with a rest. She lies down and covers her body with a blanket to keep warm. She closes her eyes, completely relaxes her arms and legs, and stays in this resting pose for several minutes.

pages.text: Jenny and her friends have finished their yoga practice. Yoga helps them feel flexible and strong!
pages.brief: Jenny and her friends stand together after finishing their yoga practice. Their bodies look flexible and strong after all the poses and breathing. They are no longer moving through the poses and have completed their yoga session.

books.title: Animals, Animals
books.art_why: The book describes real animals and natural habitats that exist today.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals in the natural world. Mammals are animals that have fur or hair. The elk is in the deer family. Male elk have large antlers, while female elk have none. Elk are excellent swimmers and can run very fast. Giraffes only live in savannas and open woodlands in Africa. Giraffes have spots all over their bodies and short horns on their heads. Giraffes are very tall with long necks.
pages.brief: A group of mammals with fur or hair includes an elk in the deer family, with a male showing large antlers and a female with none, both able to swim and run fast. Nearby, tall giraffes with spots and short horns stand in African savanna and open woodland.

pages.text: Elephants are the largest land animals alive today. Elephants have long trunks and ivory tusks. They live in grasslands and forests in Africa or Asia. They hunt wild goats, sheep, and other animals that live in their habitat. They have thick fur that is white with black spots, and it helps them stay warm. Snow leopards live on cold mountains.
pages.brief: An elephant, the largest land animal, has a long trunk and ivory tusks and lives in grasslands and forests of Africa or Asia. On a cold mountain, a snow leopard with thick white fur and black spots stays warm while hunting wild goats, sheep, and other animals in its habitat.

pages.text: This camel has a long winter coat of hair. When a camel is well fed, its humps stand up, but the humps fall to one side if the camel has not eaten. Camels live in both hot and cold deserts, such as the Gobi desert in Asia. Foxes eat small animals, insects, fruits, and eggs. A fox lives in a burrow, sometimes using one another animal had already made. Unlike dogs, foxes like to hunt alone. The fox is in the dog family.
pages.brief: A camel with a long winter coat of hair stands in a hot or cold desert such as the Gobi in Asia; its humps stand up when well fed and fall to one side when not. A fox eats small animals, insects, fruits, and eggs, lives in a burrow, and hunts alone.

pages.text: The zebra is in the horse family. Zebras have white and black stripes and live in grasslands in Africa. Their manes stand straight up on their necks like mohawks! Kangaroos eat grass and other plants. It uses its strong back legs to hop and its long tail for balance. The great gray kangaroo carries its babies in its pouch.
pages.brief: A zebra in the horse family has white and black stripes, a mane standing straight up like a mohawk, and lives in African grasslands. A great gray kangaroo uses strong back legs to hop, a long tail for balance, and carries its babies in a pouch while eating grass and other plants.

pages.text: The hippopotamus spends most of its time in water. It has very little hair and eats grass and water plants. Its eyes and nostrils stick out so that it can see and breathe when underwater. There are many kinds of animals. They eat seals, walruses, small mammals, birds, and fish. They have thick fur to keep them warm. Polar bears live in cold places in the Arctic.
pages.brief: A hippopotamus with very little hair spends most of its time in water, eating grass and water plants, its eyes and nostrils sticking out so it can see and breathe underwater. In the cold Arctic, a polar bear with thick fur hunts seals, walruses, small mammals, birds, and fish.

books.title: Hibernation
books.art_why: Real animals and real winter places that exist today can be photographed.

pages.text: Food Is Scarce Many places have cold winters. Some animals in these places have trouble finding food in the winter. Food is scarce during this time. Some animals migrate to warmer places to find food and return in the spring. Other animals hibernate to survive the winter months.
pages.brief: A cold winter landscape with snow on the ground and bare trees. A few animals search for food and find very little. In the sky a group of animals travels off toward warmer places. Nearby, one animal is curled up asleep, hidden away for the winter months.

pages.text: What Is Hibernating? Hibernation is like a very sound sleep. Not even loud noises can wake the animals up. Hibernating animals sleep for days or weeks at a time. Hibernating animals breathe very slowly. Their hearts beat slower, they are using little energy, and they do not need to eat.
pages.brief: A hibernating animal curled in a ball inside a dark den, eyes closed, sleeping very deeply. Its chest barely moves as it breathes slowly. Loud noise outside does not reach it. The animal lies still, using little energy, with no food beside it.

pages.text: When a warm-blooded animal hibernates, its body temperature drops until it is almost as cold as the temperature outside. A cold-blooded animal’s body temperature always matches the temperature outside. When a cold-blooded animal gets too cold, it hibernates.
pages.brief: Two animals in the cold: one warm-blooded, its body temperature dropping until it is almost as cold as the snowy air around it; the other cold-blooded, its body matching the outdoor temperature exactly. Frost and cold air surround both of them.

pages.text: How Do They Stay Alive? Hibernating animals eat lots of food before winter and store the food in their bodies as fat. Their bodies live off this fat while they sleep. It takes very little energy to keep hibernating animals alive.
pages.brief: An animal eating a great deal of food in autumn, nuts and seeds and berries, its body growing round and plump. A view inside its body shows the food stored as fat beneath the skin. Later it sleeps through winter, living off that fat and needing nothing to eat.

pages.text: Where Do Animals Hibernate? Hibernating animals also need a safe place to sleep. They need to be away from the cold and hidden from hungry predators. Some animals, like bats, hibernate in caves.
pages.brief: A dark cave entrance in a cold, snowy hillside. Bats hang upside down from the cave ceiling, clustered together and sleeping, away from the cold. Outside, wind blows and snow falls. The cave is hidden and safe from hungry predators.

pages.text: Hibernating snakes sleep underground in burrows. Frogs and turtles sleep in mud at the bottom of ponds. Some mice hibernate in winter nests. Some animals, like squirrels, store food where they hibernate.
pages.brief: Sleeping animals in their winter places: snakes coiled underground in burrows, frogs and turtles buried in mud at the bottom of a pond, mice curled in a winter nest, and a squirrel beside stored food where it hibernates.

pages.text: Many people think of bears when they think of hibernation, but a bear is not really a hibernating animal. A bear often wakes up and moves around in winter. Also, a bear’s body temperature doesn’t get as cold as that of other warm-blooded hibernating animals. The bear’s sleep is called a torpor. A torpor is a deep sleep, but not as deep as hibernation.
pages.brief: A bear awake outside its den in the winter snow, having woken and moved about. Its body is not as cold as a true hibernating animal's. Beside it a small warm-blooded hibernating animal sleeps far more deeply. The bear's sleep is a torpor.

pages.text: Like a hibernating animal, though, a bear prepares a place to sleep for winter. It fills its winter den with leaves and tree branches. This bed helps keep the bear’s body heat in while it sleeps. Layers of snow on the den also keep the heat inside. This helps keep the bear warm.
pages.brief: A bear inside its winter den, the floor lined with leaves and tree branches gathered into a bed. The bear curls on the leaves, its body heat held in. Outside, layers of snow pile over the den and keep the warmth inside.

pages.text: Like birds, some butterflies fly to warmer areas in winter. But many insects hibernate. They need a safe, warm place to sleep just like other hibernating animals. Some hibernate in holes in the ground, while others hibernate under tree bark. Some insects, like many ladybugs, hibernate in buildings, including houses!
pages.brief: Butterflies flying away toward warmer areas. Other insects stay and hibernate: some in holes in the ground, some under rough tree bark, and ladybugs clustered together inside a building, resting in a warm corner of a house.

pages.text: Who Hibernates? Warm-blooded animals like groundhogs, chipmunks, and prairie dogs hibernate. Cold-blooded animals like snakes, frogs, turtles, insects, and lizards hibernate.
pages.brief: Hibernating animals gathered in one scene: a groundhog, a chipmunk and a prairie dog, warm-blooded, asleep; and a snake, a frog, a turtle, an insect and a lizard, cold-blooded, sleeping in their own safe places.

pages.text: Some animals like bats, some squirrels, and some mice hibernate all winter long. Some animals wake up to eat, as bears do. Raccoons, badgers and skunks might wake up to eat on a warm winter day. In the spring, all the hibernating animals wake up.
pages.brief: Spring arrives, snow melting and green shoots appearing. Bats, squirrels and mice wake after sleeping all winter. A bear, a raccoon, a badger and a skunk stir and come out to eat on a warm day. All the hibernating animals wake up.

books.title: Bats
books.art_why: Modern bats exist today, so photographs can show real animals and their features.

pages.text: Introduction Enter a cave just as night approaches, and you might see a dark cloud pouring like smoke from the cave. It’s a cloud of sorts, but it’s not a rain cloud—it’s a “bat cloud.” Bats like to spend the daytime in the cool darkness of a cave hanging upside down from the ceiling, but nighttime is different— it is time to hunt. So thousands of bats take flight from the cave. They dive and dart about, snatching insects from the air.
pages.brief: A cave entrance at nightfall, with thousands of bats pouring out like dark smoke. Inside the cool cave, other bats hang upside down from the ceiling. Outside, the flying bats dive and dart through the air, snatching insects.

pages.text: About Bats Bats are one of the oldest groups of mammals to have lived on Earth. According to fossil records, they were sweeping through the air almost 60 million years ago. Bats flew through the Earth’s skies before humans walked on the planet. Although bats have been around for all that time, they haven’t changed much. Ancient fossils show that bats of long ago were very much like modern-day bats. There are close to 1,000 kinds of bats. In fact, there are more kinds of bats than there are kinds of any other mammal. These bats are placed into two groups— microbats and megabats.
pages.brief: A bat fossil skeleton is shown beside a modern bat, showing how much the ancient bat resembles the modern one. Around them, many different kinds of bats suggest the nearly one thousand species and the two groups, microbats and megabats.

pages.text: Microbats eat mostly insects, but some also eat small fish, mammals, and amphibians. The smallest microbat is the bumblebee bat, which is about as long as a paper clip. Microbats live in a wide range of places and can be found throughout the world.
pages.brief: A small microbat hunts insects in the night sky. Nearby, the tiny bumblebee bat is shown next to a paper clip to show its tiny length. Other microbats appear in different parts of the world, including one catching a small fish.

pages.text: Megabats eat fruits. They are found in warm, tropical areas where lots of fruit grows all year long. The largest megabat is the Malayan flying fox. It is so large that with its wings spread out, it would stretch the length of the average-sized bathtub. While some megabats are big, megabats are not always larger than microbats.
pages.brief: A megabat hangs in a warm tropical tree, eating fruit. The huge Malayan flying fox spreads its wings, which are as long as an average bathtub. Smaller megabats are nearby, showing that megabats are not always larger than microbats.

pages.text: Bat Features Bats seem to get a bad rap when it comes to looks. In fact, some people might consider them downright ugly. Others think bats look fierce and scary. If you get to know bats better, you might change your opinion of them. You might even think that some bats are rather cute.
pages.brief: A close-up of a bat's face, with soft fur and large eyes. The bat looks gentle rather than fierce or scary. Around it, a few other bats have different expressions, suggesting that people may find bats ugly, scary, or even cute once they know them.

pages.text: Bats, like most mammals, are covered with hair or fur, which is soft and quite short. There are a few types of bats that have only a little fuzz on their bodies. No wonder these bats are called naked bats. Bat fur comes in as many colors as human hair does. There are bats with brown, black, gray, red, and even yellow fur.
pages.brief: Several bats show their fur: brown, black, gray, red, and yellow. Most have short, soft fur covering their bodies. One bat has only a little fuzz, a naked bat. A close-up shows the short fur on a bat's back and head.

pages.text: Bats are the only mammals that can fly. Flying squirrels are mammals, too, but they don’t really fly. They glide through the air after jumping from a tree branch. Bat wings are made of two thin layers of skin. The skin is so thin that you can almost see through it. A bat’s wings are really modified hands that even have small thumbs. The skin stretches between long, thin bones when the bat is in flight and folds up when the wings are not in use. A bat’s wings are used for more than flying. If a bat is too warm, it stretches out its wings so heat can escape to cool the bat. If the bat is too cold, it can wrap itself in its wings.
pages.brief: A bat flies with thin wing skin stretched between long, thin bones, showing small thumbs. A flying squirrel glides from a tree branch nearby. Another bat folds its wings around itself, while one stretches its wings out to cool down.

pages.text: Like you, bats have two sets of teeth. The baby teeth are lost early in a bat’s life. They are replaced by a set of 26 to 28 adult teeth. These teeth are sharp and are used to cut and crush food. Despite what many people believe, bats aren’t blind. Bats use their eyes to see during the day and in the early evening. Let’s learn how bats find food in the dark.
pages.brief: A bat's face shows sharp adult teeth used for cutting and crushing food. The bat's eyes are open in daylight, showing that it is not blind. A small baby bat is nearby, hinting that baby teeth are lost early and replaced by adult teeth.

pages.text: Flight and Feeding Bats are skilled fliers. The bones of the bat’s wings can bend easily to change the shape of the wings. By changing the shape of their wings, bats can quickly change the direction of their flight. In addition to wings, most bats also have a piece of skin that stretches between their legs. When flying, bats spread their legs so that they can use the pouch of skin to help them steer up or down and swerve left or right. Do You Know? Bats are able to fly high and fast. Bats have been clocked going as fast as 100 kilometers per hour (62 mph). This is as fast as a car speeding down a highway. Some bats can fly 3.2 kilometers (2 mi ) high.
pages.brief: A bat flies fast and high, changing direction by bending the bones in its wings. The skin between its legs is spread wide to help it steer up, down, left, and right. The bat speeds through the air like a car on a highway.

pages.text: We now know that bats are skilled fliers. But skilled flying alone doesn’t make bats good hunters. Since bats do most of their hunting in the dark of night, they need more talents than flying in order to hunt. Microbats also have another feature to help them hunt— echolocation. This is the use of sound waves to help bats locate insects in flight. The photo and text below show how bats use echolocation. How Echolocation Works.
pages.brief: A microbat hunts at night, sending out sound waves toward an insect. The sound waves spread through the dark air and help the bat locate the insect in flight. The bat flies with skill, but echolocation is the extra talent it needs for hunting.

pages.text: When a bat finds an insect, it sends out more beeps or clicks and sends them out much faster. It might send out up to 200 beeps or clicks per second. As it closes in on its target, it sweeps up the insect with a wing and scoops it into a pouch that is formed with the skin between its legs. Later, the bat will stick its head into the pouch to gobble up the meal. Bats also snatch insects out of the air with their mouths.
pages.brief: A bat closes in on an insect and sweeps it up with a wing into the pouch of skin between its legs. Later, the bat sticks its head into the pouch to eat the meal. Another bat snatches an insect out of the air with its mouth.

pages.text: The combination of skilled flying and echolocation makes microbats excellent hunters at night. The next time you are out at night, take a look skyward. You will likely see bats darting through the air, collecting insects in their tail pouches. Observe how quickly they change direction. They are responding to brain signals telling them where food can be found. Do You Know? Some microbats eat up to 600 mosquitoes an hour, and some will eat up to 3,000 insects in a single night of hunting.
pages.brief: At night, bats dart across the sky, catching insects and collecting them in tail pouches. They change direction quickly as they hunt. Many insects fill the air around them, suggesting the hundreds of mosquitoes and thousands of insects that some microbats eat in one night.

pages.text: Bat Behavior Bats are not the mean, frightening creatures that many people think they are. They don’t get into your hair or attack people, and there are no human vampires that turn into bats. The truth is that bats are shy, gentle creatures. In fact, bats are our friends. Just think of how many insects would be around if it were not for bats.
pages.brief: A shy, gentle bat hangs quietly in a sheltered place. It does not look mean or frightening. Around it, many insects fly in the night air, showing how many insects there might be if bats were not around to eat them.

pages.text: Can you imagine sleeping while hanging upside down with blood rushing to your head? Well, it’s not a problem for bats. Bats sleep upside down. They cling to the undersides of surfaces using the claws on their toes. Hanging upside down makes it easy to take off to fly. All they have to do is let go and begin flapping their wings.
pages.brief: A bat hangs upside down from the underside of a surface, clinging with the claws on its toes. Its body is upside down, but it looks comfortable. It is ready to let go and begin flapping its wings to take off into flight.

pages.text: Many bats hibernate in the winter when there are no insects to hunt. Before hibernating, bats eat lots of food, which they store as extra fat. They depend on this fat to survive during the winter. Some bats migrate to warmer areas during the winter. Red bats fly all the way from Canada to Mexico rather than spend the winter in the cold. There is even a bat in Europe that flies over 1,600 kilometers (1,000 mi) to spend the summer in Russia. Don’t expect to see bats migrating, since they fly at night.
pages.brief: A bat hibernates in winter, its body carrying extra fat stored from eating lots of food. Another bat flies at night on a long migration to a warmer place. A red bat travels from Canada to Mexico, while a European bat flies far to Russia for summer.

pages.text: Female bats give birth to one or two babies every year. They are the only flying animals that nurse their young on milk. After a baby bat is born, it crawls up to its mother’s chest and clings there with its claws. It feeds off its mother’s milk and even clings to the mother’s fur when she goes hunting. But baby bats don’t hang around for long. Many are able to fly and catch their own meals only three weeks after birth. Do You Know? Some bats are threatened by a deadly disease. White-nose Syndrome has killed more than a million bats in thirteen states since it was first discovered in 2006.
pages.brief: A female bat hangs upside down with a baby clinging to her chest and fur, feeding on her milk. Nearby, another bat has a white nose, showing the deadly disease called white-nose syndrome that has killed many bats in thirteen states since 2006.

pages.text: Tr y This! Building a Bat House.
pages.brief: A bat house is introduced as a building project. Show a simple wooden bat house as the focus, with a small shelter shape for bats. Keep the scene focused on the bat house itself, without adding people, tools, or extra instructions.

pages.text: 4. Nail the boards together as shown. 5. Hang your bat house high in a tree or on the side of a building. Hang it where it is not too sunny.
pages.brief: Boards are joined together to form a bat house, then the finished bat house is hung high in a tree or on the side of a building. It is placed in a spot that is not too sunny.

books.title: Wonders of Nature
books.art_why: All subjects are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Wonders of Nature.
pages.brief: A calm, open nature scene with natural light and open space, kept broad and simple for a cover image. No people, animals, or events appear; the view stays quiet and general rather than showing a specific habitat or creature.

pages.text: Introduction The world is full of strange and interesting animals. Some animals look unusual or have special abilities. Let’s look at some of these wonders of nature.
pages.brief: A wide natural view shows several strange and interesting animals with unusual looks or special abilities in different outdoor places. Some stand, perch, or rest among plants and water, presenting the variety of animal life without any people in the scene.

pages.text: Archerfish Archerfish spit drops of water at insects and spiders to knock them off leaves and branches near the water. Archerfish have very good aim and can squirt water over long distances. When the bugs fall into the water, the archerfish eat them. Archerfish may also leap all the way out of the water to catch bugs.
pages.brief: An archerfish floats at the water surface near leaves and branches. It spits a drop of water at an insect or spider on a leaf above, aiming carefully. Another archerfish leaps clear of the water to catch a bug near the surface.

pages.text: Trap-Door Spider A trap-door spider lives in a sticky underground tunnel with a hidden door made of silk and dirt. The silk in the door helps keep water out of the spider’s tunnel when it rains. When an insect passes close to the door, the trap-door spider senses its movements and jumps out to grab it.
pages.brief: A trap-door spider waits inside its sticky underground tunnel, hidden behind a door made of silk and dirt. Rainwater stays outside. An insect passes close to the hidden door, and the spider senses the movement and jumps out to grab it.

pages.text: Beaver Beavers chew through tree trunks with their sharp teeth. They build large dams in rivers and streams using the tree trunks, branches, mud, clay, and stones. Beavers build their homes, which are called lodges, in the ponds formed by the dams. By creating ponds, beavers change the landscapes of the areas they live in. The wetlands that beavers create with their dams become home to many other animals.
pages.brief: Beavers chew through tree trunks with sharp teeth beside a river or stream. Using trunks, branches, mud, clay, and stones, they build a large dam. In the pond behind it, a beaver lodge sits among the wetland that other animals share.

pages.text: Chameleon Chameleons are lizards that can change color to hide. When the air gets warmer or colder, their skin changes color. They even change color to show how they feel. Chameleons catch insects with their long tongues, which can be twice as long as their bodies. Chameleons can point each of their eyes in a different direction at the same time to help them see all around them. When they spot an insect they want to eat, chameleons focus both of their eyes forward to help them aim their tongues.
pages.brief: A chameleon clings to a branch, its skin changing color with the air’s warmth or its feelings. One eye points in one direction and the other eye another way. It focuses both eyes forward and shoots its long tongue at an insect.

pages.text: Flying Dragon Flying dragons are small lizards that can glide through the air from tree to tree. They have folds of skin on the sides of their bodies that open like wings. The wings are brightly colored and have spots and stripes on them. Flying dragons use their sticky tongues to catch and eat insects, mainly ants and termites.
pages.brief: A flying dragon, a small lizard, glides from one tree to another. Folds of skin along its sides open like brightly colored wings with spots and stripes. Below and around it are trees and air, showing how it moves through the air without falling.

pages.text: Leaf Insect Leaf insects are usually found in the tropical areas of Asia. Their bodies, wings, and legs look like leaves, which allows them to blend in with real leaves on trees. Their eggs look like seeds. The eggs can take more than a year to hatch. Baby leaf insects are red, but when they start eating leaves, they turn green.
pages.brief: A leaf insect rests on a leafy tree in tropical Asia. Its body, wings, and legs look like real leaves, helping it blend in. Nearby, its eggs look like seeds. A baby leaf insect is red before it starts eating leaves and turns green.

pages.text: Leaf-Rolling Weevil In the summer, the female leaf-rolling weevil rolls a leaf into a cone shape. She can take up to two hours getting the leaf just right. She lays her eggs inside the cone and then closes the open end. When the leaf falls to the ground in autumn, it carries the eggs with it. The leaf hides and protects the eggs until they hatch. When the larvae hatch, they eat the dead leaf.
pages.brief: A female leaf-rolling weevil works on a plant in summer, rolling a leaf into a cone shape. She lays eggs inside and closes the open end. Later the leaf falls to the ground in autumn, carrying the eggs, and larvae eat the dead leaf after hatching.

pages.text: Praying Mantis The praying mantis often holds its front legs in a praying position. Mantises hide on plants to catch their food. Some mantises are green to blend in with leaves, and some that live in the desert are the color of sand. The praying mantis eats many types of insects as well as small frogs, lizards, and mice. Praying mantises can even catch and eat small birds such as hummingbirds.
pages.brief: A praying mantis hides on a plant, holding its front legs in a praying position. Its green body blends with leaves. Nearby are insects, small frogs, lizards, mice, and a hummingbird, all foods the mantis can catch and eat.

pages.text: Mole Moles burrow underground to find and eat earthworms. They also eat beetles, slugs, and snails. A mole digs many connected tunnels, creating a maze. It builds its nest deep in these tunnels. Because its fur points up, a mole can move backward and forward in a tunnel without getting dirt trapped in its coat. Moles have tiny eyes, but they are not blind.
pages.brief: A mole digs through connected underground tunnels that form a maze. It searches for earthworms, beetles, slugs, and snails. Deep in the tunnels is its nest. Its tiny eyes are open, not blind, and its fur points up as it moves forward and backward without trapping dirt.

pages.text: Sea Dragon Sea dragons are small fish that are related to sea horses. Their bodies have many parts that look like the stems and leaves of seaweed. They blend in with ocean plants, which helps them catch food and hide from enemies. Sea dragons use small, clear fins on their necks and backs to swim. The female lays eggs on the male sea dragon’s tail, and the male carries the eggs until they hatch.
pages.brief: A sea dragon swims among ocean plants that look like seaweed. Its body has parts resembling seaweed stems and leaves, helping it blend in. Small, clear fins on its neck and back move it along. A male carries eggs attached to his tail.

pages.text: Conclusion Interesting animals come in many shapes and sizes. Their special looks and abilities help them to survive. All these animals are wonders of nature.
pages.brief: A wide nature scene brings together animals of many shapes and sizes in their habitats. Each one shows a special look or ability that helps it survive. No people appear, and the view presents the animals as wonders of nature.

books.title: Baltic Rescue
books.art_why: The story is a real modern animal rescue involving a real dog and research ship, so photographs fit.

pages.text: One cold winter day, a dog walked to the edge of an icy river in Poland. Nobody knows for sure where the dog came from or what he was doing there. But he was about to have a big adventure.
pages.brief: A lone dog stands at the edge of an icy river in Poland on a cold winter day. The dog is alone, looking toward the frozen water. No people are visible nearby; the dog's origin and purpose are unknown as he begins an unexpected adventure.

pages.text: Without warning, the ice that the dog was standing on broke away from the land. The dog was swept down the river on a sheet of ice half the size of a football field. The frightened dog looked for a way to get back to the shore, but he was trapped on the ice. The river was too cold for him to swim to safety.
pages.brief: The ice beneath the dog breaks away from the land. The frightened dog stands on a large floating sheet of ice, about half the size of a football field, drifting down the river. He looks toward the distant shore, trapped, with cold water all around.

pages.text: Some firefighters saw the dog drifting down the river as he passed through their city. They tried to help him, but they couldn’t reach him. The firefighters could only watch as the ice carried the dog farther down the river.
pages.brief: Firefighters in a riverside city see the dog drifting past on the ice. They stand at the water's edge and try to reach him, but the gap is too wide. They can only watch as the ice carries the dog farther down the river.

pages.text: For three days, the dog drifted down the river on his raft of ice. He passed through several more towns. At least one other group of people saw him and tried to help him. But they weren’t able to reach him, either.
pages.brief: For three days, the dog drifts down the river on his raft of ice. He passes several towns along the banks. At least one other group of people spots him and tries to help, but they cannot reach the floating dog either.

pages.text: Each day, the hungry dog grew colder, weaker, and more scared. His ice raft was slowly melting and breaking up into hundreds of smaller pieces. By now, the piece he was standing on was not much larger than a small bedroom. If he slipped off, he might become trapped under one of the many chunks of ice around him and drown.
pages.brief: The hungry dog looks colder, weaker, and more scared as days pass. His ice raft is melting and breaking into hundreds of smaller pieces. The piece under him is now about the size of a small bedroom, surrounded by dangerous chunks of ice.

pages.text: POLAND GERMANY On the fourth day, the dog passed the mouth of the river and was swept out into the Baltic Sea. He had traveled more than 75 miles (120 km) from where he began. He was moving farther away from land and any hope of rescue. The piece of ice he was standing on had shrunk to the size of a picnic table.
pages.brief: On the fourth day, the dog is swept past the river's mouth and out into the Baltic Sea. He has traveled more than 75 miles from where he began. The ice beneath him has shrunk to the size of a picnic table, and land is far away.

pages.text: The dog was facing a deadly end to his adventure, but his luck was about to change. Some scientists and sailors aboard a research ship named the Baltica were passing through the area. They saw an animal moving on the ice in the distance and decided to investigate.
pages.brief: The dog is alone on a small piece of ice in the open sea, nearing a deadly end. A research ship carrying scientists and sailors passes through the area. They spot a small animal moving on distant ice and turn to investigate. The dog remains alone on his shrinking ice floe.

pages.text: At first, the people on the ship thought the animal was a seal. They were amazed when they got closer and saw that the “seal” had four legs, floppy ears, and a tail. They had found a dog floating on the ice 15 miles (24 km) from land!
pages.brief: From the research ship, the people first mistake the distant animal for a seal. As they get closer, they are amazed to see four legs, floppy ears, and a tail. It is a dog floating on the ice, 15 miles from land.

pages.text: The Baltica ’s sailors were able to bring their ship close to the dog. They lowered a net next to the dog, but he was too scared to climb into it. The dog even slipped and fell into the cold water while they were trying to help him. Luckily, he was able to climb back onto the slippery ice.
pages.brief: The ship's sailors move the vessel close to the dog and lower a net beside him. The scared dog will not climb in and slips into the cold water. He manages to scramble back onto the slippery ice as the crew tries to help.

pages.text: Fearing that the dog would drown, the crew lowered a raft. Adam, the ship’s mechanic, used the raft to get close to the dog. Adam grabbed the dog by the back of the neck and pulled him into the raft.
pages.brief: Fearing the dog will drown, the crew lowers a raft. Adam, the ship's mechanic, guides the raft close to the ice. He grabs the dog by the back of the neck and pulls him safely into the raft.

pages.text: Once the dog was safe aboard the ship, the crew dried him and wrapped him in blankets. They rubbed him with towels to warm him up. At first, the dog was too weak to stand. He curled up and went to sleep on a blanket. After a good nap, the dog was strong enough to join the crew for breakfast and eat some sausages.
pages.brief: Safe aboard the ship, the crew dries the dog and wraps him in blankets, rubbing him with towels to warm him. Too weak to stand, he curls up and sleeps on a blanket. After a good nap, he joins the crew for breakfast and eats sausages.

pages.text: The crew named the dog Baltic after the name of the sea where they rescued him. Once the ship returned to port, they took Baltic to a veterinarian. The vet made sure Baltic hadn’t suffered any serious injuries from his icy adventure. The crew also searched for Baltic’s owners for several weeks but couldn’t find them. Adam, the sailor who pulled Baltic into the raft, decided to adopt him.
pages.brief: The crew names the dog Baltic after the sea where he was rescued. Back at port, a veterinarian checks him and finds no serious injuries. The crew searches for his owners for weeks without success, so Adam, the sailor who pulled him into the raft, adopts him.

pages.text: Now, Baltic is the mascot of the research ship that found him and travels with the crew everywhere. He has many fans around the world who learned about his incredible journey and rescue. The president of Poland even wrote a letter to the crew of the ship, praising them for saving Baltic’s life. Baltic started out cold, wet, and alone on the ice but ended up warm, dry, and surrounded by new friends.
pages.brief: Baltic, now the research ship's mascot, stands with the crew on deck. Around the world, fans follow his story. In Poland, the president honors the crew for saving Baltic, who began cold, wet, and alone but now is warm, dry, and surrounded by friends.

books.title: Jane Goodall
books.art_why: Real photographs of Jane Goodall, chimpanzees, and Gombe exist.

pages.text: The Watcher Jane Goodall was born in England in 1934. As a child, she liked to learn about animals. She liked to watch how they behaved. Jane loved to read colorful stories about wild animals. She dreamed of living in Africa. Jane was sure that, one day, she wanted to live with animals and write stories about them.
pages.brief: A young Jane Goodall in England in the 1930s, watching animals closely and reading colorful storybooks about wild animals. She looks thoughtful as she dreams of Africa, imagining herself living among animals and writing stories about them.

pages.text: Off to Africa When Goodall finished school, she went to work in an office. She saved the money she earned. When she had saved enough, Goodall took a trip to Kenya, in Africa. In Kenya, she met Dr. Louis Leakey. Leakey was a scientist who wanted to learn how apes might be like humans.
pages.brief: A grown Jane Goodall working in an office and saving money, then traveling to Kenya in Africa. There she meets Dr. Louis Leakey, a scientist studying how apes might be like humans, in a simple meeting setting.

pages.text: Dr. Leakey hired Goodall to work with him. One day, he talked about doing a new kind of study. The study would be about chimpanzees in Tanzania (tan-zuh-NEE-uh). Dr. Leakey was looking for someone to watch how the chimps lived and report on them. He asked if Goodall would like to be that person.
