pages.brief: Dr. Louis Leakey hires Jane Goodall to work with him. He describes a new study of chimpanzees in Tanzania and asks whether she would be the person to watch how the chimps live and report on them.

pages.text: Into the Forest Goodall moved to Gombe (GOME-bay), a forest in Tanzania. She watched the chimps every day. She wrote careful notes about what she saw. Goodall saw that the chimps lived in family groups. In her notes, she gave each family member a name.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall moves into the Gombe forest in Tanzania, watching chimpanzees every day and writing careful notes. She observes the chimps living in family groups and gives each family member a personal name in her notes.

pages.text: The Gombe Gang At first, many of the chimps were afraid of Goodall. An older chimp she named David trusted her, though. One day, David let Goodall meet his family group. She watched them and wrote reports on how they behaved. Her reports upset many old beliefs about chimps. The Woman Who Named Things Some scientists doubted Goodall’s findings. They didn’t believe that chimps had feelings or were very smart. They certainly didn’t think a serious scientist should give personal names to the animals she studied.
pages.brief: In the Gombe forest, many chimpanzees keep their distance from Jane Goodall, but an older chimp named David trusts her. David lets her meet his family group, and she watches them and writes reports on how they behave.

pages.text: At the time, most people believed that chimps ate only plants. Goodall saw David’s family eat meat. Most people believed chimps weren’t smart enough to use simple tools. Goodall saw David use a stick to poke into a termite hill to reach a termite snack. That was smart! Goodall reported that David used the stick as a tool to get food. Her words upset many scientists because they thought only people could make or use tools.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall watches David's family eat meat and sees David poke a stick into a termite hill to reach a termite snack. She reports that he uses the stick as a tool, surprising scientists who thought only people could make or use tools.

pages.text: Other chimps also began to trust Goodall and let her watch them. She reported chimp behavior that no one else had ever seen before.
pages.brief: More chimpanzees begin to trust Jane Goodall and allow her to watch them in the forest. She observes and reports chimp behavior that no one else has ever seen before, recording their actions carefully as they go about their days.

pages.text: Goodall said that each chimp behaved in its own way, just as humans do. She saw chimps being happy, sad, angry, and loving—just as humans are. Goodall’s reports surprised many people. Her work made many scientists think that their old ideas about the species might be wrong.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall explains that each chimpanzee behaves in its own way, just as humans do. She sees chimps being happy, sad, angry, and loving, and her reports surprise many people and make scientists question their old ideas about the species.

pages.text: Trouble in the Forest After living in Gombe for many years, Goodall began to worry. Many people in this part of Africa are very poor. Some were cutting down the forest for firewood or to grow crops there. The chimps were losing their homes. Some people were even hunting the chimps. Hunters stole baby chimps to sell them.
pages.brief: After many years in Gombe, Jane Goodall worries as people cut down forest for firewood and crops, and chimpanzees lose their homes. Some hunters even steal baby chimps to sell, putting the Gombe chimps in serious danger.

pages.text: Goodall was afraid that the Gombe chimps might all die. She knew she had to tell people what was happening in the Gombe Forest. Goodall began to travel and talk with large groups of people. She asked them to help her save the chimps and the forest. People trusted Goodall and listened to her. They agreed to support her work in Gombe.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall fears the Gombe chimps might all die, so she travels and speaks to large groups of people. She asks them to help save the chimps and the forest, and people trust her, listen, and agree to support her work in Gombe.

pages.text: The Work Goes On More than sixty years have passed since Jane Goodall first went to Tanzania. With the help of many, the work she started there continues. Jane Goodall died on October 1, 2025 at the age of ninety-one. She will be remembered for her work to protect chimps and their habitats. She changed the way that people view all animals.
pages.brief: More than sixty years after Jane Goodall first went to Tanzania, the work she started continues with help from many people. She is remembered after her death at ninety-one for protecting chimps and their habitats and for changing the way people view all animals.

pages.text: Goodall visits a chimp rescue center in Uganda in 2018. Jane Goodall Programs Sadly, chimp numbers in Gombe and much of Africa continue to drop. The work to protect them continues, however. In 1977, Goodall began the Jane Goodall Institute This institute gives money to scientists who study chimps in the wild. It also teaches people living near wild places how to help protect the wildlife in their area. In 1991, Goodall began Roots & Shoots The Roots & Shoots program began in Tanzania with just twelve local teens. Today, it operates in more than 130 countries and has thousands of members. Its main goal is to educate young people about problems that exist right around them. To learn more, go to: www.rootsandshoots.org and www.janegoodall.org.
pages.brief: Jane Goodall visits a chimp rescue center in Uganda in 2018, standing near rescued chimps. Nearby, a group of young people and scientists represent her Jane Goodall Institute and Roots & Shoots programs, which teach people to protect wildlife.

books.title: Owls Overhead
books.art_why: Owls and their habitats exist in the real world today.

pages.text: Flying in the Moonlight It’s a moonlit night. A dark shape floats over you and into the trees. It’s an owl!
pages.brief: On a moonlit night, a dark owl shape floats overhead and glides into the trees. The sky is bright with moonlight, and the owl’s silent dark form passes above the viewer before disappearing among the branches.

pages.text: More than two hundred different kinds of owls live around the world. The way they look and act helps them survive.
pages.brief: More than two hundred kinds of owls live around the world. A group of different owls appears in varied natural settings, each with its own look and way of acting that helps it survive in its home.

pages.text: Eyes for the Night Owls can’t move their eyes, so they turn their heads. Owls can turn their heads almost all the way around. They can even turn their heads upside down!
pages.brief: An owl turns its head almost all the way around, its large eyes staying fixed because they cannot move. The owl twists its neck in a tree, showing it can even turn its head upside down.

pages.text: Owls have big eyes, but they can’t see in total darkness. They see better in low light than most animals, though. That’s because of their pupils—the black circles in the center of their eyes. Their pupils can grow large to let in more light.
pages.brief: A close view of an owl’s face shows its big eyes and the black pupils in the center. The owl sits in dim light, where its pupils can grow large to let in more light than most animals’ eyes.

pages.text: Even Better Ears Most owls use their hearing to hunt. Owls have huge ears. On most owls, one ear is higher than the other. Owls can hear prey that’s hiding in grass or snow.
pages.brief: Most owls use their hearing to hunt. An owl stands alert with huge ears, one set higher than the other, its face turned as it listens closely for prey hidden in grass or snow nearby.

pages.text: Owls, such as this barn owl, often crush their prey. The grip of some owls can be ten times stronger than a person’s grip. Pellets! Owls can’t chew their food. Instead, they often swallow animals whole. A part of their stomach rolls unwanted animal parts into small balls called pellets. A few hours after they eat, owls cough up a pellet. Barn owls can hear a mouse and catch it in complete darkness. Barn owls have the best hearing of any animal.
pages.brief: A barn owl stands in complete darkness, gripping prey with strong talons while a small pellet rests nearby. Its face turns as it listens for a mouse, using hearing that is the best of any animal.

pages.text: Silent Hunters Owls must attack by surprise if they want to eat. The soft feathers that cover their bodies help them fly without a sound.
pages.brief: An owl glides low through a quiet night, its soft feathers spread wide for soundless flight. It approaches a small hidden animal by surprise, its body streamlined and ready to attack without making a sound.

pages.text: The main food for most owls is small animals—lots of them. In its lifetime, a barn owl may eat 11,000 mice!
pages.brief: A barn owl stands surrounded by many small mice, the main food for most owls. Over its lifetime, this barn owl may eat 11,000 mice, so the ground around it is crowded with tiny prey.

pages.text: Where Owls Live Some owls can live in many different places. Other owls cannot. An Owl’s Housekeeper Screech owls hunt snakes. However, they bring the blindsnake back to their nest alive. They let it go inside the nest, where it eats the bugs that feed on the dead animals stored there. The snake becomes a housekeeper!
pages.brief: A screech owl brings a live blindsnake to its nest. Inside, the snake moves among stored dead animals, eating the bugs that feed there while the owl watches. The snake acts as the owl’s housekeeper.

pages.text: Spotted owls can only survive in old forests with huge trees. Many of these forests have been cut down. Today, few spotted owls are left.
pages.brief: A spotted owl perches in an old forest among huge trees, its spotted feathers blending with bark. Nearby, cut stumps show where many forests have been cut down, leaving few spotted owls in the remaining trees.

pages.text: Owls Are Out There People don’t see owls very often, but they are out there. Go out at sunset and listen for their calls. If you stay out too late, people might think you’re an owl. A night owl, that is.
pages.brief: At sunset, a child stands outdoors, listening for owl calls. An owl is partly hidden in nearby trees, hard to see. The scene shows that people rarely spot owls, though the birds are out there.

pages.text: Owl Sounds Owls aren’t always quiet. They all make different sounds. A great horned owl can bark like a dog and meow like a cat. Barn owls don’t hoot—they scream.
pages.brief: A great horned owl opens its beak to bark like a dog and meow like a cat, while a barn owl nearby screams instead of hooting. Together they show that owls make many different sounds.

books.title: China
books.art_why: The book reaches back to China's ancient civilization, the first paper and gunpowder, and the Silk Road, none of which a camera could capture.

pages.text: China Where Is It? The People’s Republic of China is one of the biggest countries in the world. Along with Russia, it makes up a big part of Asia. Many other countries share a border with China.
pages.brief: A wide view of Asia seen from high above, with China's huge land spread across the middle, Russia filling the north, and many smaller neighbouring countries running along China's long borders. Mountains, deserts and green plains show how big the land is.

pages.text: Beijing is the capital of China. The city is more than three thousand years old. More than fifteen million people live there.
pages.brief: A busy street in Beijing: tall modern buildings stand beside older tiled rooftops, and crowded pavements and roads are full of people and bicycles. Residents of all ages go about their day in the capital city, which is more than three thousand years old.

pages.text: People More than one billion people live in China. More people live in China than in any other country in the world. Seven out of ten Chinese people speak Mandarin. People also speak many other languages, including English. Chinese writing does not use the letters of the English alphabet. Instead, it uses thousands of characters that stand for words or parts of words.
pages.brief: A crowded city square filled with Chinese people of all ages — families, workers and children talking together. Nearby, a person carefully writes Chinese characters with a brush on paper, making word-pictures instead of letters from the English alphabet.

pages.text: Some people live and work in the tall buildings in China’s big cities. Others live on small farms and grow food. More people live in towns and villages than in other places.
pages.brief: Two scenes side by side: office workers inside tall glass buildings in a big city, and a family on a small farm tending rows of vegetables. Low houses of a village and a small town sit nearby in the countryside.

pages.text: Celebrations The Chinese New Year is one of the biggest celebrations in China. It takes place in late January or early February. Many cities hold parades. People dress up in colorful costumes. Some people dress up as lions or dragons. Many Chinese people believe lions and dragons bring good luck. People often shoot off fireworks, too.
pages.brief: A Chinese New Year parade moves through a city street in late January or early February. Dancers in colourful lion and dragon costumes leap and sway, crowds in bright clothing watch and cheer, and fireworks burst in the sky above the rooftops.

pages.text: History China has one of the oldest civilizations still around today. Experts think it began more than five thousand years ago. The ancient Chinese people created many things we still use today. They were the first to create paper. They were also the first to make gunpowder. We still use gunpowder in fireworks today.
pages.brief: Ancient Chinese scenes: a scholar presses wet pulp flat to make the first sheet of paper, while a worker mixes the first gunpowder in a stone bowl. Behind them, an old walled settlement shows a civilization more than five thousand years old.

pages.text: Chinese people also discovered how to make silk cloth. Long ago, people came to China from far away places to buy silk cloth. The road they used was called the Silk Road.
pages.brief: Workers unwind silk threads from cocoons and weave soft silk cloth on a wooden loom. Outside, a long caravan of camels and traders loaded with rolls of silk travels a dusty road toward China from faraway places, coming to buy the cloth.

pages.text: China’s Landforms Land China is so large that it has many different types of land. The north is mostly desert. The south has some of the tallest mountains in the world.
pages.brief: Northern China: dry sand dunes stretch under a hot sky with almost no plants. Far to the south, snow-capped peaks of the world's tallest mountains rise above cloud and rocky valleys, showing two very different kinds of land in one country.

pages.text: In other parts of China, forests cover the land. China also has large wetlands and flat areas covered with grass. Much of this land is used to grow food.
pages.brief: Tall trees fill a green forest, then wide wetlands with shallow water and reeds where birds wade, then flat grassland stretching to the horizon. On part of the grassy land, farmers plant and tend crops in rows to grow food.

pages.text: Animals Many people know of giant pandas and Siberian tigers. Giant pandas live in bamboo forests in a small area in the center of China. They eat only bamboo. Siberian tigers are among the largest cats in the world. They live in the forests in the east and the south of China. Both Siberian tigers and giant pandas are in danger of dying out. However, many people are working to protect them.
pages.brief: A giant panda sits in a bamboo forest in the centre of China, chewing bamboo stalks. In forests to the east and south, a large Siberian tiger walks between the trees. People are working nearby to protect both kinds of animal.

pages.text: Conclusion China is a large country. Many different people and animals live in this land. People from all over the world come to explore China each year. If you were to visit China, what would you most like to see?
pages.brief: Visitors from around the world arrive in China: travellers with backpacks and cameras step off a train into a busy city, gaze up at mountains, and watch pandas, all exploring this large land and wondering what they would most like to see.

books.title: India
books.art_why: Modern India is a real place today, so photographs can show its people, land, and animals.

pages.text: India Afghanistan China Bhutan Pakistan New Delhi Nepal India Myanmar (Burma) Bangladesh ARABIAN SEA Mumbai Bay of Bengal Andaman ASIA Sri Lanka Nicobar INDIAN OCEAN Where Is It? India is a country in Asia. Much of it is surrounded by water. To the south and west is the Arabian Sea. To the south and east is the Bay of Bengal.
pages.brief: A map of India in Asia shows the country surrounded by the Arabian Sea to the south and west and the Bay of Bengal to the south and east, with neighboring countries around it on land.

pages.text: The capital of India is New Delhi (DEL- ee). It is part of the much larger city of Delhi. More than twenty million people live in Delhi and New Delhi.
pages.brief: New Delhi, the capital of India, is part of the much larger city of Delhi, where more than twenty million people live in crowded city areas with many buildings and busy streets all around.

pages.text: People More than one billion people live in India. Only China has more people than India. The cities do not have as many people as the countryside. They are very crowded, though.
pages.brief: Many people live in India, more than one billion, with crowded cities and a countryside that holds even more people; only China has more people than India in a wide, busy scene.

pages.text: Around half of the people in India make their living from growing food. They grow crops or raise sheep, goats, and chickens for meat. Many Indians are Hindu. Some Hindus consider cows to be sacred and do not eat beef. They raise cows to plow their fields. People in India have used elephants to carry crops and do other kinds of work for a long time.
pages.brief: Farmers grow crops and raise sheep, goats, and chickens; some Hindus treat cows as sacred and use cows to plow fields, while elephants carry crops and do other work for a long time in the fields around them.

pages.text: India’s Landforms Indus River Himalayan Mtns. Mount Everest New Delhi Indo-Gangetic Plain Thar Desert Ganges River India Chota Nagpur Plateau Sundarban Deccan Plateau Western Ghats Mtns. Eastern Ghats Mtns. Land India has many mountains and kinds of flat land. Some mountains are in the north. They are the highest in the world.
pages.brief: A landform map of India shows the Himalayan Mountains and Mount Everest in the north, the Indus and Ganges rivers, the dry Thar Desert in the west, the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Chota Nagpur and Deccan plateaus, the Western and Eastern Ghats, and the Sundarban.

pages.text: Rich land covers the north of India. It was formed long ago as rivers flooded over and over. In the west is the dry desert. In the south are hills and lakes. This land takes up more than half of India. In May or June every year, winds bring a large amount of rain. This is called the monsoon season. Most of India’s rain falls during this season.
pages.brief: A wide view of India’s land shows rich northern plains beside a river, the dry western desert, southern hills and lakes, and dark monsoon clouds bringing heavy rain over the land in May or June.

pages.text: Celebrations People in India celebrate many special days. Diwali (dee-VAH-lee) lasts for five days. During this festival, people light small candles. They shoot firecrackers and give sweets to family and friends.
pages.brief: A family and friends celebrate Diwali for five days, lighting small candles, shooting firecrackers, and giving sweets to one another in a warm, festive gathering full of light and color together. The scene feels joyful.

pages.text: Holi (HOH-lee) is a spring Hindu festival. During Holi, people celebrate the end of winter. They throw colored water and powder on each other.
pages.brief: People celebrate Holi, a spring Hindu festival marking the end of winter, by throwing colored water and powder on each other in a lively outdoor scene, with bright colors filling the air around them together.

pages.text: Animals Many kinds of animals live in India. It is the only country in the world with both lions and tigers. Elephants live in the flat lands and forests. The mountains are home to bears, foxes, sheep, and wild goats.
pages.brief: Many animals live in India: a lion and a tiger share the country, elephants move through flat lands and forests, and bears, foxes, sheep, and wild goats live in the mountains in a wide natural scene.

pages.text: India is also home to the world’s largest mangrove forest. Here, tigers swim with sea turtles, sharks, and crocodiles.
pages.brief: In the world’s largest mangrove forest, a tiger swims in the water with sea turtles, sharks, and crocodiles around it, showing the rich life of this forest and its water in the natural scene together.

pages.text: Conclusion India is a country of many people. People farm its rich soil to feed the nation. Its mountains and forests are home to many animals. Which part of India would you like to see?
pages.brief: A wide view of India shows many people, farmers working rich soil to grow food, and mountains and forests that are home to wild animals across the country in one broad, peaceful, natural scene together.

books.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
books.art_why: Trees, leaves, animals, and people exist in the real world and can be photographed.

pages.text: So Many Colors One of nature’s most beautiful sights is a forest full of bright fall colors. Imagine making art with all those colors of paint!
pages.brief: A forest full of bright fall colors spreads across the scene, with red, orange, and yellow leaves on many trees. Splotches of paint in the same colors sit nearby, suggesting making art from those autumn shades.

pages.text: Leaves in their fall colors are beautiful. Did you ever wonder why a tree’s leaves change color? To answer this question, you need to understand the important job that leaves do. Two Types of Trees Not all trees lose their leaves in fall. Deciduous (dee-SIJ-oo-us) trees lose their leaves once each year, but evergreen trees lose and grow their leaves throughout the year. This book is about deciduous trees.
pages.brief: Colorful fall leaves hang on a deciduous tree, while an evergreen tree nearby stays green. Some leaves drift down from the deciduous tree, and the evergreen keeps its leaves through the year. The two kinds of trees grow in the same woodland.

pages.text: Making Food Leaves make food so the tree can grow and have energy. This process is called photosynthesis. Leaves need four things to do their job. 1) Leaves need water, which they get from the tree through their stems.
pages.brief: On a tree branch, a green leaf is attached to a stem. Water moves from the tree through the stem and into the leaf, helping the leaf make food for the tree. Sunlight falls on the leaf as it works.

pages.text: 2) Leaves also need a gas called carbon dioxide. They take in carbon dioxide from the air around them. 3) All plants use a chemical called chlorophyll for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll gives leaves their green color. Many parts of green plants have some chlorophyll in them. Leaves have the most chlorophyll of all the parts.
pages.brief: Green leaves on a plant take in carbon dioxide from the air around them. Chlorophyll fills the leaves and gives them their green color. Other green parts of the plant also contain some chlorophyll, but the leaves have the most.

pages.text: 4) Leaves need sunlight for photosynthesis. Sunlight and chlorophyll work together to turn water and carbon dioxide into a kind of sugar. This sugar is the food that gives plants energy. When they make food, trees also give off a gas called oxygen that animals and people need to live.
pages.brief: Sunlight shines on a green leaf as water and carbon dioxide move into it. The leaf makes sugar for food, and oxygen drifts out into the air. A child and a small animal nearby breathe the oxygen they need.

pages.text: Photosynthesis doesn’t just help plants stay alive. Photosynthesis makes food for all living things. Some animals, such as mice, eat plants. Other animals, such as hawks, eat the plant eaters. Without plants, what would hawks do for food?
pages.brief: A mouse nibbles a green plant, and a hawk perches nearby, watching. The plant made food through photosynthesis, the mouse eats the plant, and the hawk eats plant eaters. Without plants, the hawk would have no food.

pages.text: Summer Summer is playtime for some people. For the leaves of many trees, however, it’s work, work, work! The Sun is shining, and the leaves are making sugar from water, carbon dioxide, and sunlight.
pages.brief: On a sunny summer day, people play outdoors while green leaves on a tree work. Sunlight shines on the leaves, and they use water, carbon dioxide, and sunlight to make sugar. The summer sun is bright above them.

pages.text: What do the leaves do with the sugar? They send it to the tree’s roots, branches, and buds. Those parts store sugar so the tree will have food during the cold months. Wowser! Most trees that drop their leaves lose them over days, weeks, or even months. However, a ginkgo tree can lose all its leaves in a single day.
pages.brief: Green leaves send sugar through the tree to its roots, branches, and buds, which store food for the cold months. Nearby, a ginkgo tree stands with many leaves that can all fall in a single day.

pages.text: Leaves are green in summer because they are full of chlorophyll. Leaves also have orange, yellow, or brown chemicals inside them. Those chemicals are there in summer, but the green chlorophyll hides them. Do You Know? The chemical that makes leaves orange is also found in carrots, tomatoes, and sweet potatoes. The chemical that makes leaves red is also found in berries, cherries, plums, and red cabbage.
pages.brief: Green summer leaves on a tree are full of chlorophyll. Hidden inside the leaves are orange, yellow, and brown chemicals. Carrots, tomatoes, sweet potatoes, berries, cherries, plums, and red cabbage show the same orange and red chemicals.

pages.text: Fall In places far from Earth’s equator, the temperature gets cooler in fall. The days get shorter, and the nights get longer. Trees get less sunlight, so photosynthesis slows down. Over time, leaves stop making chlorophyll, so they lose their green color. The hidden orange, yellow, and brown colors start to show. Leaves also start making a red chemical during the fall. Bright Red Leaves The red color in leaves comes from sugar that gets trapped in the leaves. Some trees, such as red maples, make more red color than other trees. How red the leaves turn also depends on the weather, so some years have a lot more red leaves than other years.
pages.brief: In fall, cooler air and shorter days reach a forest far from the equator. Green chlorophyll fades from the leaves, showing orange, yellow, and brown. Some trees, such as red maples, make bright red leaves, and weather affects how red they turn.

pages.text: When the weather gets cold enough in fall, the temperature drops below freezing. Since tree sap contains a lot of water, it can freeze. A tree’s roots, trunk, and branches protect the sap from freezing. However, leaves are very thin. If they freeze, the tree will be hurt. Trees drop their leaves to keep themselves safe. They close off the opening at the bottom of each leaf’s stem, and soon afterward, the leaves fall off.
pages.brief: Cold fall air below freezing surrounds a tree with thin leaves. The tree protects its watery sap in roots, trunk, and branches. It closes off the bottom of each leaf stem, and soon the leaves fall to the ground.

pages.text: Winter and Spring Trees that drop their leaves are bare in winter. They use the stored food to get through the cold days and colder nights. When spring arrives, ice and snow melt, and the rains come. The Sun shines, and tiny leaves sprout from branches. Once again, the leaves use water, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide, and sunlight to make food. The cycle begins again.
pages.brief: A bare tree stands in winter cold, using stored food. Then spring arrives: ice and snow melt, rain falls, the Sun shines, and tiny green leaves sprout from the branches, ready to make food again. The cycle starts again.

books.title: Giant Pumpkins
books.art_why: Real giant pumpkins, growers and contests exist today.

pages.text: Giant Pumpkins Have you ever seen a pumpkin so big it would not fit in a car? People all over the world have taken up the hobby of growing giant pumpkins. Growers compete against one another, hoping to break the record for the world’s biggest pumpkin. In 2013, Tim Mathison from Napa, California, won with a pumpkin that weighed 2,032 pounds (922 kg). That’s how much a walrus or a small car weighs! The gigantic squash measured more than 17 feet (5.2 m) around.
pages.brief: Tim Mathison from Napa stands in a garden beside an enormous orange pumpkin that is wider than a small car parked nearby. The record-breaking pumpkin rests on the ground, showing its gigantic size and more than seventeen-foot circumference.

pages.text: World’s Biggest Pumpkin Mathison grew three giant pumpkins over six months in 2013. His pumpkins set world records for the first-, third-, and fourth-largest pumpkins ever grown. Mathison won more than $50,000 in prizes for his pumpkins. He showed his record-breaking pumpkin to the world on a national television show. While growing them, his daughter, Tara, joined her dad in the pumpkin patch every evening. Tara cannot walk or talk because of a rare medical problem.
pages.brief: Tim Mathison stands in a pumpkin patch with three giant pumpkins; his daughter Tara joins him there in the evening. In another scene, he displays his record-breaking pumpkin on a national television show after winning more than $50,000 in prizes for pumpkins that set world records.

pages.text: “She is my inspiration,” Mathison said. “I took her out to the patch every night for two hours, and she’d be smiling.” Mathison’s giant pumpkins got bigger every year. He said using the best seeds, soil, and plant food was his secret. Mathison shares the seeds from his winning pumpkins with growers all over the world. He hopes kids will grow their own giant pumpkins. “It’s amazing to watch the pumpkins grow,” he said. “Some days they put on 53 pounds (24 kg). It’s a lot of fun.”
pages.brief: At dusk, Tim Mathison tends his giant pumpkins with his daughter Tara beside him, smiling. He holds pumpkin seeds to share with growers, and large pumpkins grow on strong vines around them. Some pumpkins grow rapidly, putting on many pounds in a single day.

pages.text: Growing a Winner According to Mathison, anyone can grow giant pumpkins. They just have to understand what pumpkins need. Pumpkin growers make sure their soil is rich with nutrients. They use compost in the soil. Rich soil helps pumpkins grow quickly. Growers use seeds that are known to produce giant pumpkins. They plant them indoors in the spring, often in April. The plants can be hurt by cold or heat, so they must be protected.
pages.brief: A grower prepares rich dark soil with compost in a garden bed. Giant-pumpkin seeds are planted indoors in small pots during spring, often April, and young seedlings sit protected from cold and heat in a bright indoor space.

pages.text: Mathison used heaters to give his pumpkins a “head start” in the spring of 2013. Once it was warmer, the plants were moved to a sunny spot in the garden. Then they were carefully watered and fertilized. Growers prune the plants, or cut away extra vines. They do this at least every other day. When flowers appear, they are pollinated. Then the pumpkins start to grow. The best pumpkins grow on strong, healthy vines. Growers are careful not to use too much plant food. Pumpkins can grow too big and burst.
pages.brief: Tim Mathison tends young pumpkin plants in a sunny garden, with a heater nearby giving them a head start. He waters and fertilizes the plants, cuts away extra vines, and pollinates a flower. A small pumpkin begins growing on a strong vine, while he measures plant food carefully so pumpkins do not burst.

pages.text: When they are the size of softballs, all but the best pumpkins are cut off the vine. As a result, the plant food reaches the most perfect pumpkins. Mathison spent two hours every morning working in his pumpkin patch. After he came home from work, he spent two more hours in the garden every evening. He fertilized, pruned, and cared for his four pumpkin plants all summer and into the fall.
pages.brief: Tim Mathison kneels in his pumpkin patch, cutting extra softball-sized pumpkins from a vine so one perfect pumpkin remains. He works among four pumpkin plants in the morning and again in the evening, fertilizing, pruning and caring for them through summer and into fall.

pages.text: There Can Be Only One! In October, growers with the biggest pumpkins meet at weigh-offs. It is an exciting time as growers wait to see who has the biggest pumpkin. For winners, the long months of planning, planting, pruning, watering, and care pay off. Their giant pumpkins are some of the biggest in the world!
pages.brief: At an October weigh-off, growers with enormous pumpkins gather and wait eagerly to see whose pumpkin is biggest. The winning grower stands beside a giant pumpkin after months of planning, planting, pruning, watering and care. Several huge pumpkins fill the contest area.

pages.text: Growers use forklifts and trucks to transport their pumpkins to weigh- offs. They use ropes, straps, and chains. Pumpkins are weighed on giant scales to see which is the biggest. After the contests are over, growers have creative, yummy ways of using their pumpkins.
pages.brief: Workers use a forklift and truck to move a giant pumpkin, securing it with ropes, straps and chains. At the weigh-off, the pumpkin sits on a giant scale. Later, a grower cuts up the pumpkin in a kitchen to make creative, yummy food.

pages.text: Pumpkin Boats Some growers scoop out their giant pumpkins and turn them into boats. People use paddles to race the boats. Sometimes they wear costumes during the races. A man in the United Kingdom set a new speed world record in 2013. In two minutes he paddled a giant pumpkin 100 meters. That is about the length of a football field.
pages.brief: A person in a costume paddles a hollowed-out giant pumpkin boat across water, racing other pumpkin boats. A man paddles a giant pumpkin at high speed, covering 100 meters in two minutes, about the length of a football field.

pages.text: Gigantic Jack-o’-Lanterns Giant pumpkins can be carved into silly or scary jack-o’-lanterns. Some carvers use power tools to create works of art.
pages.brief: A carver uses a power tool on a giant pumpkin, cutting a silly or scary face into it. The finished jack-o’-lantern displays the carved design, and other giant carved pumpkins sit nearby as works of art.

pages.text: Wowser! The recipe for the giant pumpkin pie called for 2,796 eggs, 525 pounds (238 kg) of sugar, 7 pounds (3.1 kg) of salt, and 14.5 pounds (6.6 kg) of cinnamon. Giant Pumpkin Pie! Some giant pumpkins are used to make huge pies. Growers of giant pumpkins in Ohio baked a pie that was named the world’s largest in 2010. It was 20 feet (6.1 m) wide and weighed 3,699 pounds (1,678 kg). That’s a lot of pumpkin pie!
pages.brief: Growers in Ohio stand beside a huge pumpkin pie named the world's largest in 2010. The pie is 20 feet wide and weighs 3,699 pounds. Around it are large amounts of eggs, sugar, salt and cinnamon used in the giant recipe.

pages.text: Growing giant pumpkins can be fun. Maybe someday you will grow the world’s biggest pumpkin in your backyard!
pages.brief: A child kneels in a backyard garden beside a young pumpkin plant, with a big orange pumpkin nearby. The child looks at the growing pumpkin, showing how much fun growing giant pumpkins can be; perhaps someday this child will grow the world’s biggest.

books.title: It's Time for the Park
books.art_why: Present-day city parks, real people and ordinary daily activities are photographed in real life.

pages.text: It’s Time for the Park.
pages.brief: A city park in the soft light of early morning, before anyone has arrived. Wide paths, open grass and leafy trees are seen from the entrance, everything still and quiet. Nothing is happening yet; the park waits for its busy day to begin.

pages.text: There are parks in almost every city. At this park, it is early morning. The park is waking up. It opens at six o’clock. In every park, many things happen at different times during a day. From six o’clock to half past six, many runners come to this park. They like to run while it is still cool. It is just before eight o’clock. Aiyana, Laura, and their mother walk through the park on their way to school. Aiyana wants to stop and watch the pigeons and squirrels. But Mom and Laura pull Aiyana along. The girls must not be late for school. They know that the bell rings exactly at eight o’clock.
pages.brief: Early morning in a city park: adult runners jog along a path in the cool air. Later, just before eight, Aiyana and Laura walk to school with their mother; Aiyana turns toward pigeons and squirrels on the grass while Mom and Laura pull her along so the girls are not late.

pages.text: It is a quarter past eight. The park is quiet in the morning. Bev looks over some homework she has done. It is nice to study outside in the sun. At a quarter to nine, Bev leaves the park. She has to get to school. The gardener gets to the park early. She picks up her tools and gets right to work. At nine o’clock, the gardener begins to weed the gardens. There are four small flower gardens in the park. She spends fifteen minutes weeding each one. There are a lot of weeds, and it is starting to get hot. She weeds for one hour. She stops to take a break at ten o’clock.
pages.brief: At a quarter past eight the park is quiet. Bev sits outside in the sunshine looking over her homework, then packs up and leaves for school. A gardener arrives early, picks up her tools and weeds four small flower gardens, fifteen minutes each, working an hour until her ten o'clock break.

pages.text: Laila comes to the park every morning at about the same time. Sometimes she plays with friends. Sometimes she has fun with just her dad and her mom. This morning, Laila arrives at twenty minutes after ten. She and her parents leave the park at ten minutes to twelve. Jason and Jenny meet in the park for lunch. Jason brings picnic food with him. They have only an hour for lunch. Jason left work at twelve o’clock. He and Jenny reach the pond at eleven minutes after twelve. They sit on the grass near the pond to eat. At fourteen minutes before one, Jason looks at his watch. He and Jenny need to get back to work.
pages.brief: Laila plays in the park with her mom and dad during the morning, arriving at twenty past ten. Later Jason and Jenny meet for lunch: Jason carries picnic food, they reach the pond at eleven minutes past twelve and sit on the grass to eat, and Jason checks his watch before they go back to work.

pages.text: A family from out of town visits the park. At 1:00, they find the oldest tree in the city. At 1:15, they watch the small children in the playground. At 1:30, they cool off their feet in the fountain. At 1:45, they leave the park. They don’t want to leave, but there are so many other places to visit on their vacation. The park is very busy in the afternoon. People walk dogs and play sports. They enjoy the sunshine and relax in the shade. A group comes to the park at two o’clock to do yoga. The group does yoga until three o’clock.
pages.brief: A visiting family finds the oldest tree in the city at one o'clock, watches small children in the playground, cools their feet in the fountain and leaves at a quarter to two. The busy afternoon park holds people walking dogs, playing sports, resting in shade, and a group doing yoga from two until three.

pages.text: Anton comes to the park right after school to play chess. He arrives at the park at three o’clock. He plays some practice games. Then his friend, Mr. Fox, gives him a lesson. Anton leaves the park at six o’clock. When the weather is warm, people play soccer in the park. Today, two teams of children are playing. Their game starts at six o’clock. They play for one and a half hours.
pages.brief: After school Anton arrives at the park at three o'clock and plays practice chess games before his friend Mr. Fox gives him a lesson; he leaves at six. On the warm grass two teams of children play soccer, their game starting at six and lasting an hour and a half.

pages.text: Greg leaves home at seven o’clock. He meets his friends by the pond. They race their boats on the water. They use remote controls to steer their boats. After the races, Greg goes home. He gets back home at 8:15. Notes.
pages.brief: In the evening Greg leaves home at seven o'clock and meets his friends beside the pond, where they race small boats on the water, steering them with remote controls. After the races Greg walks home and is back at his house at a quarter past eight.

books.title: Hoover Dam
books.art_why: Hoover Dam exists today and can be photographed.

pages.text: A Mighty Dam When Hoover Dam was built in the 1930s, it was the tallest dam in the world. The dam is as tall as a sixty-story building! Hoover Dam is on the Colorado River. The dam controls the flow of the river’s water. The dam’s power plant uses the water to make electricity.
pages.brief: A wide view of Hoover Dam across the Colorado River, with the dam rising very high and holding back the river’s water. Its power plant sits near the dam, using the flowing water to make electricity.

pages.text: Dry Desert Hoover Dam is on the border between Arizona and Nevada. It is about 30 miles (48 km) from the city of Las Vegas. Hoover Dam is in a very dry desert. The dam is in a deep, narrow valley between mountains. Hoover Dam Nevada Utah Colorado California Arizona New Mexico.
pages.brief: Hoover Dam sits in a dry desert valley between mountains, on the border between Arizona and Nevada. The city of Las Vegas is about 30 miles away. The dam stands in the deep, narrow valley, with desert land and mountain slopes around it.

pages.text: Strong Dam, Huge Lake The Colorado River flows downhill to Hoover Dam. The dam stops the water from flowing quickly. Water collects above the dam to form Lake Mead. It is the biggest lake in the United States made by people.
pages.brief: The Colorado River flows downhill toward Hoover Dam. Above the dam, water spreads out and collects into Lake Mead, a huge lake made by people. The dam holds the water back, and the lake stretches wide behind it.

pages.text: Water has a lot of force when it flows downhill. Hoover Dam is very heavy so it can stay strong when the water hits it. The dam is curved to move the water to the two sides of the canyon. A power plant near the dam changes the force of the moving water into electricity. downstream gravity arch upstream Hoover Dam’s shape and size help hold the water back.
pages.brief: A close view of Hoover Dam’s curved shape holding back water in a canyon. Heavy water presses against the dam, which is built to stay strong, while its power plant turns the force of moving water into electricity. The dam’s size and curve help move water to the canyon sides.

pages.text: Solving a Problem People have been growing crops along the Colorado River for many years. The river used to flood in spring and wash away the crops. People built dams on the river to stop the flooding. Hoover Dam was the first of those dams.
pages.brief: People grow crops along the Colorado River in earlier times. In spring, the river floods and washes the crops away. Dams built on the river hold back the floodwater, and Hoover Dam is the first of those dams.

pages.text: Building the Dam The project began in 1931. Workers had to make the river go around where Hoover Dam would be built. They dug four tunnels, and they also built huge walls above and below where the dam would be. After they finished, the water flowed into the tunnels and out lower down. Then workers moved rocks and mud away to make room for the dam.
pages.brief: Workers begin the Hoover Dam project in 1931. They dig four tunnels and build huge walls above and below the dam site so the river can go around it. Water flows into the tunnels and out lower down while workers move rocks and mud to make room.

pages.text: Workers used giant molds to build the dam. They dumped huge buckets of concrete into each mold. Cold water ran through small pipes so each block of concrete would cool quickly. After each block was cool, workers built another block on top of it. Later, they sealed the stacks of blocks with grout.
pages.brief: Workers use giant molds to build Hoover Dam block by block. They dump huge buckets of concrete into each mold, and cold water runs through small pipes so the concrete cools quickly. After each block cools, workers add another on top and seal the stacks with grout.

pages.text: Hoover Dam If the river ever flooded, the water would ruin the power plant. Workers built two places for the water to go if it got very high. Those places are called spillways. Finally, workers built the power plant and four towers. The towers control how much water goes to the power plant at a time.
pages.brief: Hoover Dam’s power plant sits beside the river, with two spillways built so high water can go around it instead of ruining the plant. Workers also build the power plant and four towers. The towers control how much water goes to the power plant at a time.

pages.text: All the work was finished in 1936. The project took about five years. Building Hoover Dam was hard, unsafe work. Many workers lost their lives during the project.
pages.brief: The completed Hoover Dam is shown after the project finished in 1936, about five years after it began. Workers are at the hard and unsafe construction site, where many workers lost their lives during the project.

pages.text: Seeing the Dam Millions of people see Hoover Dam every year. The visitor center has displays about the area and how the dam was built. People can go inside the dam and power plant. At Lake Mead, they can go fishing and boating. Take a camera if you go. There’s a lot to see!
pages.brief: Many visitors see Hoover Dam each year. The visitor center has displays about the area and how the dam was built. People go inside the dam and power plant, and at Lake Mead they fish and boat. A camera is shown because there is a lot to see.

pages.text: Hoover Dam Today Hoover Dam changed many people’s lives. The river’s water helps crops grow in dry areas of the United States. The power plant makes electricity for over a million people. Other dams have been built on the Colorado River since the 1930s. But Hoover Dam was the first, and it’s still the biggest!
pages.brief: Hoover Dam stands today on the Colorado River. Its water helps crops grow in dry areas of the United States, and its power plant makes electricity for over a million people. Other dams have been built on the river since the 1930s, but Hoover Dam remains the first and biggest.

books.title: Nature Stinks!
books.art_why: Real plants and animals that exist today can be photographed.

pages.text: Nature Stinks!
pages.brief: An opening page introduces the idea that nature can stink. It shows only a plain, simple background because this page names no particular plant, animal, person or place, leaving the stinky nature topic open for the pages that follow.

pages.text: Stinky Nature If you’ve ever smelled a skunk, you know it is not a nice odor. In fact, it’s terrible! Did you know that both plants and animals can smell bad? Stinky plants smell bad to get helpful insects to come near. Stinky animals often smell bad to keep enemies away. Smelling bad helps both plants and animals stay alive.
pages.brief: A skunk releases a terrible odor. Nearby, a stinky plant gives off a bad smell that brings helpful insects close, while a bad-smelling animal uses its odor to keep enemies away. Smelling bad helps both plants and animals stay alive.

pages.text: Stinky Furry Animals Skunks are well-known for being smelly animals. When enemies get too close, skunks lift their tail and spray a stinky liquid. Striped polecats are cousins of skunks, and they stink even worse!
pages.brief: A skunk lifts its tail and sprays a stinky liquid toward enemies that get too close. Nearby, a striped polecat, a cousin of the skunk, is shown as an even stinkier animal. Both animals use a terrible smell for defence.

pages.text: Lesser anteaters are at least four times as stinky as a skunk! They shoot a smelly liquid at their enemies. Opossums pretend to be dead if an enemy is nearby. They remain still and release stinky green slime.
pages.brief: A lesser anteater shoots a smelly liquid at an enemy. Nearby, an opossum lies still and pretends to be dead while releasing stinky green slime. Both animals use bad smells to defend themselves when threatened.

pages.text: Wolverines make a smelly liquid to keep other animals away from their home. They also pee on food they don’t eat right away. The smell may help them find the food later, and it may also prevent other animals from eating it.
pages.brief: A wolverine makes a smelly liquid to keep other animals away from its home. It also pees on food it does not eat right away. The smell may help the wolverine find the food later, and it may stop other animals from eating it.

pages.text: Male musk oxen fight each other for females. Males use their stinky pee to tell other males to keep away. The pee sticks to their long belly hair and makes them smell terrible.
pages.brief: Two male musk oxen face each other and fight over females. One male's stinky pee sticks to its long belly hair, making the musk ox smell terrible and telling other males to keep away from the females.

pages.text: Stinky Plants The corpse flower smells rotten. It makes heat and steam so insects far away will smell it. The plant’s bad smell brings flies and beetles near because these insects are looking for rotten meat to eat. Although they don’t find any meat, the bugs collect powder from the flower and carry it to other corpse flowers. The powder helps more corpse flowers grow. A different stinky plant smells like poop! This plant’s bad smell brings beetles that love poop. The smell comes from inside the plant’s flowers.
pages.brief: A corpse flower gives off a rotten smell and makes heat and steam that carry the odor to flies and beetles. The insects look for rotten meat, find none, and carry powder to other corpse flowers. Another stinky plant smells like poop and attracts beetles that love poop from inside its flowers.

pages.text: Stinky Birds The stinkbird mainly eats leaves. Food goes to its crop (the area under its throat) before the stomach. Tiny living things in the crop break down the leaves. This way of eating makes the stinkbird smell terrible.
pages.brief: A stinkbird eats leaves. The food goes into its crop, the area under its throat, before reaching its stomach. Tiny living things in the crop break down the leaves, and this way of eating makes the stinkbird smell terrible.

pages.text: Vultures eat animals that are dead and often rotten. When vultures are in danger, they throw up! The stuff they throw up is very smelly.
pages.brief: A vulture stands near a dead, rotten animal it eats. When the vulture is in danger, it throws up, and the stuff it throws up is very smelly. The bad smell is part of how it stays safe.

pages.text: Stinky Bugs A type of beetle sprays a hot, stinky liquid from the back of its body. The spray can kill many enemies and burn people.
pages.brief: A beetle sprays a hot, stinky liquid from the back of its body toward an enemy. The spray can kill many enemies and can burn people. It uses this powerful defense when it is threatened by danger.

pages.text: Millipedes (MILL-ih-peedz) can’t move fast to get away from enemies. If an enemy bothers them, they curl up and give off a stinky liquid. Some millipedes can even shoot the smelly stuff!
pages.brief: A millipede curls up after an enemy bothers it, since it cannot move fast to get away. It gives off a stinky liquid, and some millipedes can even shoot the smelly stuff at enemies to escape.

pages.text: Other Stinky Animals The common musk turtle has another name—stinkpot! It smells bad when other animals disturb it. A stinky yellow liquid comes out of the back of its body. The mink frog also uses a smell like rotten onions to stay safe from its enemies.
pages.brief: A common musk turtle, also called a stinkpot, releases a stinky yellow liquid from the back of its body when other animals disturb it. Nearby, a mink frog gives off a smell like rotten onions to stay safe from its enemies.

pages.text: Protecting the Nest The green woodhoopoe lives in Africa. The female makes a bad smell to protect her nest. She sprays a dark, stinky liquid to keep enemies from getting too close. Good and Stinky Being stinky helps many plants and animals stay alive. For plants, the bad smell brings helpful insects. For animals, the bad smell may keep enemies away or help in other ways. Stinky steam, spray, throw-up, slime, and pee all help living things stay alive.
pages.brief: A female green woodhoopoe in Africa sprays a dark, stinky liquid to keep enemies from getting too close to her nest. Nearby, plants and animals show how bad smells help them stay alive: plants attract helpful insects, animals keep enemies away, and stinky steam, spray, throw-up, slime and pee all help.

books.title: Earth's Water
books.art_why: Water, ice, clouds, and people are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: A wide view of distant Earth from space in sunlight shows the blue planet’s oceans, swirling white clouds, and brown landmasses against dark space, introducing the water that covers and surrounds much of the world.

pages.text: Water Everywhere Water fills oceans, lakes, and ponds. It flows in rivers, streams, and underground. It is even in the air. Some parts of Earth have snow and ice, which are frozen water.
pages.brief: Oceans, lakes, and ponds are filled with water; rivers and streams flow across the land; water moves underground and is present in the air. Snow and ice cover some parts of Earth as frozen water.

pages.text: Water covers most of Earth’s surface. Most of Earth’s water consists of salt water in the oceans. Earth has much less fresh water, and many plants and animals need this fresh water to survive. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: A broad view of Earth’s surface shows salt water oceans covering most of the planet, with much smaller areas of fresh water on land. Plants and animals gather near fresh water, which they need to survive.

pages.text: Some of this fresh water is aboveground, while other fresh water is underneath Earth’s surface. What are some ways you use Earth’s water?
pages.brief: A cutaway view of land shows fresh water aboveground in a lake and a flowing river, and fresh water underground within soil and rock. The scene invites viewers to think about ways people use Earth’s water.

pages.text: Different Forms of Water Liquid water is the most common state of Earth’s water. It takes the shape of the container that holds it. Liquid water is always moving, even if you can’t see it move. It flows in rivers and streams, and it swells and crashes as ocean waves. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Liquid water fills a container and takes its shape, while a river and a stream flow across land and ocean waves swell and crash. The water is always moving, even when the motion is hard to see.

pages.text: Not all water is in a liquid state. When liquid water gets very cold, it freezes to form ice. Ice is another state of water— solid water. Ice can float on liquid water. People form ice into different shapes. Artists even carve ice to make sculptures.
pages.brief: A block of ice floats on liquid water. Nearby, people shape ice into different forms, and an artist carves an ice sculpture with tools. The solid water holds its own shape in a cold setting.

pages.text: Much of Earth’s frozen water is at the North and South Poles, which are Earth’s coldest areas. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Wide fields of ice and snow stretch across the North Pole and South Pole, Earth’s coldest areas. Much of the planet’s frozen water sits in these bright polar regions under pale skies and cold light.

pages.text: Some of Earth’s water is in an invisible state as a gas called water vapor. While it’s always invisible, water vapor is all around us.
pages.brief: A clear outdoor scene in daylight shows a wide, calm, quiet landscape with open, empty air and no visible vapor. The air itself holds invisible water vapor, a gas that is present everywhere around us.

pages.text: Changing Water Earth’s water is always changing from one state to another. When frozen water is heated, it melts and becomes liquid water. When liquid water is cooled, it freezes and becomes ice. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: A block of ice sits beside liquid water. Heat melts the frozen water into liquid, while cold turns liquid water back into solid ice. The same water changes from one state to another in a simple cycle.

pages.text: Liquid water can become a gas, too. Have you ever seen a puddle of water dry up on a hot day? Energy from the Sun changed the liquid to a gas in a process called evaporation. Water evaporates from oceans, rivers, lakes, and puddles all over the world.
pages.brief: The Sun shines brightly on a small puddle, which dries up on a hot day. Water also evaporates from oceans, rivers, and lakes all over the world as energy from the Sun changes liquid water into gas.

pages.text: When water vapor in the air cools down, it changes from a gas to a liquid. This process is called condensation. Clouds are made up of tiny drops of water formed by condensation. The tiny drops stick together, creating larger, heavier drops. Once they’re large enough, they fall to the ground as rain or another type of precipitation. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Clouds form high in the sky as water vapor in cool air condenses into tiny drops. The drops stick together and grow larger and heavier until they fall to the ground as rain or another kind of precipitation.

pages.text: Water Is Important Rain keeps plants alive and allows them to keep growing. People and other animals need water to survive. We also use it for other purposes, such as fighting fires.
pages.brief: Steady rain falls on green plants outdoors, helping them stay alive and keep growing. Nearby, people and other animals drink clear water to survive. Firefighters use water from hoses to fight a tall, blazing fire.

pages.text: It is important to take care of Earth’s water. Keeping waste and trash away from water keeps it from becoming dirty and unusable. Polluted water makes people, plants, and animals sick. Would you want to drink and play in polluted water? Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: People pick up waste and trash near a river or lake, keeping it away from the water. Polluted water looks dirty and makes people, plants, and animals sick, while clean water is safer for drinking and playing.

books.title: Dogs at Work
books.art_why: Real dogs and real jobs can be photographed.

pages.text: Dogs at Work or or at at.
pages.brief: A group of dogs of different breeds stand together outdoors, alert and ready. Their ears are up and their noses are forward, suggesting they are workers with powerful senses. The open, clear setting introduces dogs that have jobs.

pages.text: or at at.
pages.brief: A calm dog stands in an open outdoor space, alert and quiet. Its ears are up and its nose is forward, and no other action is shown. This simple scene leads into the book about dogs at work.

pages.text: Introduction You probably know that some dogs aren’t just pets—they hold jobs! What makes dogs good workers? They learn fast, and they also hear and smell better than we do. This means that dogs can do jobs that people can’t. Some of their jobs may surprise you.
pages.brief: Several dogs of different breeds stand together outdoors, alert and attentive. Their ears are up and their noses are forward, showing how dogs learn fast and use their senses. The group suggests dogs can do jobs people cannot.

pages.text: Service and Therapy Dogs Dogs called therapy dogs work with people to help them feel better. They comfort people and keep them calm. These dogs need to be very friendly, and they are also trained to be calm around new places and people.
pages.brief: A friendly therapy dog sits calmly beside a person in a new place. The dog stays close and gentle, comforting the person and helping them feel better. Its relaxed posture shows it is trained to be calm around people and unfamiliar surroundings.

pages.text: Other dogs, called service dogs, help people with disabilities. Service dogs can do many different jobs. For example, guide dogs help people who cannot see well. These dogs are trained to keep people from stepping into traffic and to lead their owner around so that they won’t trip or fall. Tennille the Guide Dog Guide dogs can help their owner have adventures. A guide dog named Tennille helped her owner hike. Tennille was the first guide dog trained to do this. Her owner, Trevor Thomas, is blind. Tennille helped Thomas over and around large rocks. Thomas hopes that he and Tennille can encourage other blind people to follow their example.
pages.brief: Tennille, a guide dog, leads Trevor Thomas, a blind hiker, along a rocky outdoor trail. She guides him over and around large rocks. Trevor walks with her, trusting her to help him navigate the adventure.

pages.text: Some service dogs help people who can’t hear well. These dogs listen for noises, touch their owner, and move toward the noise. Other service dogs help their owner move around and do certain tasks. They pull wheelchairs, pick up dropped items, press buttons, and open doors.
pages.brief: A service dog stands beside its owner and touches the person's leg, turning toward a sound. In the same scene, another service dog pulls a wheelchair and opens a door for its owner. The dogs show different ways they help people.

pages.text: Some service dogs can smell when their owner is about to be sick. For example, dogs can be trained to smell low blood sugar. These dogs can smell changes in blood and warn their owner to eat food or take medicine. Other dogs can smell when a person is about to have a seizure. These sudden attacks cause body spasms and other problems, but service dogs can warn the person before it happens.
pages.brief: A service dog sniffs near its owner and gives a warning look. The owner reaches for food or medicine, ready to act after the dog's alert. The dog stays close, showing how it can sense a change before sickness happens.

pages.text: Search-and-Rescue Dogs Some dogs, called search-and-rescue dogs, work to find people who are lost or trapped. Many search-and-rescue dogs use their nose to find people who need help. Some of these dogs are trackers who put their nose to the ground to follow a smell.
pages.brief: A search-and-rescue dog moves through woods with its nose close to the ground, tracking a scent. The dog is following a smell to find someone lost or trapped. Its lowered head and focused steps show the work of a tracker.

pages.text: Other dogs search for missing people by sniffing the air instead of the ground. These dogs often work in a big search area and can find lost hikers using only their nose. They can also find people trapped in buildings that have fallen down.
pages.brief: A search-and-rescue dog stands in a wide outdoor search area, nose lifted, sniffing the air. In the distance, a fallen building shows where people could be trapped. The dog uses only its nose to search for lost hikers and trapped people.

pages.text: Some search-and-rescue dogs work in the water by pulling people to safety or pulling small boats to land. Water rescue dogs need to be strong swimmers. For this reason, big dogs like the Newfoundland make good water rescue dogs. These dogs have webbed toes and fur that keeps out water. Plus, they are very strong. A 68-kilogram (150 lb.) Newfoundland can pull ten people to safety at once!
pages.brief: A large Newfoundland water rescue dog swims strongly in the water, pulling a small boat toward land. Its thick, water-resistant fur and webbed toes show how it works in water. The strong dog helps people to safety.

pages.text: Odd Jobs Dogs are good learners, and they can be trained to do very unusual jobs. For example, one dog who worked at an airport in Michigan had a job chasing wild birds out of the path of planes on runways. Another group of dogs had an unusual job at a baseball park near the ocean in San Francisco. These dogs jumped into the ocean to get balls that were hit into the water. This program is now over, but for a time, baseball fans loved to collect these “Splash Hit” balls.
pages.brief: On an airport runway in Michigan, a dog runs after wild birds to clear them from a plane's path. In another scene at a baseball park by the ocean in San Francisco, a dog leaps into the water to retrieve a hit ball while fans watch.

pages.text: Detection Dogs Some dogs, called detection dogs, work as detectives. They help people find things that are hidden. Police use detection dogs in many situations. When a building has burned down, it may be hard to find out whether someone started the fire on purpose. Police use detection dogs to sniff for chemicals that might have been used to start the fire. Police also use detection dogs to find criminals.
pages.brief: A detection dog works with a police officer at a burned building, sniffing the rubble for chemicals that might show how the fire started. The dog's nose helps find hidden clues in the damaged scene.

pages.text: Police and security officers at airports also use detection dogs. These dogs search for items that are illegal to bring to another country or on a plane. They can sniff out these things in people’s bags. Other detection dogs search for termites in houses and other buildings. Termites damage buildings by eating wood. They are hard for humans to find, but these dogs can find them with their nose.
pages.brief: At an airport, a detection dog sniffs people's bags for items that are illegal to bring on a plane or into another country. In another building, a detection dog sniffs wood to find termites hidden inside.

pages.text: Conclusion Dogs do many different jobs to help humans, from sniffing out termites to pulling a swimmer to safety. Dogs are strong, smart, and friendly, and they have powerful senses. They are some of the best workers around.
pages.brief: A strong, friendly dog stands beside a swimmer it has pulled to safety, while another dog sniffs wood for termites. Around them, working dogs show different jobs, strong senses, and the many ways they help humans.

books.title: I Collect That!
books.art_why: Collecting, collectors, objects, and museums all exist in the real world.

pages.text: Introduction Do you own a few stuffed animals or video games? Then you have a collection!
pages.brief: A young collector shows a few stuffed animals and video games arranged together at home, presenting them as a collection. The child stands beside the items, looking at them with interest in a simple collection display.

pages.text: A collection is a group of objects that are alike. People collect all sorts of things, including rocks, stickers, and postcards from different places.
pages.brief: People display collections of alike objects: rocks, stickers, and postcards from different places. Several collectors arrange their items in groups so each collection shows similar things gathered together. The objects rest in sorted piles around them.

pages.text: Collecting Is Cool Collecting things is a great hobby. People collect things that excite them and keep their interest. People have different interests. Some people like action figures, while others prefer leaves.
pages.brief: People pursue collecting as a hobby. One collector examines action figures with excitement at a table, while another looks closely at leaves nearby. Their different interests show how collecting can hold attention and keep people engaged.

pages.text: Collections can be big or small. One person might have one hundred toy cars, while another might have twenty sports cards.
pages.brief: Two collectors show collections of different sizes. One person has one hundred toy cars arranged together, while another has twenty sports cards displayed in a smaller group. The two collections sit side by side for comparison.

pages.text: Collecting can bring people together. Meeting and talking to people who collect the same things can help you gain more information about your collection. You can also buy, sell, and trade parts of your collection. Do You Know? Collectors often get together at meetings called conventions. Large conventions take place around the world for collectors of all types of things—from dollhouses to toy trains.
pages.brief: Collectors meet and talk at a convention, gathering around tables. Some buy, sell, and trade parts of their collections. Nearby displays include dollhouses and toy trains, showing the wide range of things collectors bring together at large conventions.

pages.text: Maintaining a collection requires some effort. Many collectors like to care for their collections. They keep count of what they own and keep their objects clean. In addition, they usually sort their collection, such as by age, size, or type.
pages.brief: A collector cares for a collection at a table. The person keeps count of the objects, cleans them, and sorts them into groups by age, size, or type. The collection is arranged neatly as the collector handles the maintenance work.

pages.text: Common Collections Stamps, coins, trading cards, and dolls are some of the most popular things people collect. These items are often easy to find, and there are many different kinds. Math Minute Emma has 34 bookmarks in her collection. She gets 11 more for her birthday. How many bookmarks does she have now?
pages.brief: A display shows popular collections: stamps, coins, trading cards, and dolls. Nearby, Emma counts her bookmarks, with thirty-four in her collection and eleven more she received for her birthday. The bookmarks are spread out as she works out the total.

pages.text: Some people collect things from places they visit. When they go on a vacation they buy a keepsake to remind them of that place. It might be a magnet, mug, or item of clothing with the name and picture of the place. Other people collect things they find in nature, such as sticks and shells.
pages.brief: A vacationer holds keepsakes bought from a place they visited: a magnet, a mug, and an item of clothing. In another area, a nature collector gathers sticks and shells found outdoors. Both collections preserve reminders of places and natural finds.

pages.text: Many people use their collections to make new things. Some collectors make works of art, such as a map made out of bottle caps. Others make jewelry, like a necklace or bracelet made from sea glass.
pages.brief: Collectors use collections to make new things. One person creates a work of art—a map made from bottle caps. Another makes jewelry, including a necklace or bracelet from sea glass. The finished pieces show collections turned into art.

pages.text: You Collect What? Some people collect different things based on a theme. One woman’s collection of eighteen thousand owls is a world record. She has many different owl things, including T-shirts, stuffed animals, and more. Wowser! Barney Smith opened the Toilet Seat Art Museum in Texas to display the more than one thousand toilet seats in his collection. They aren’t regular toilet seats—they’re works of art!
pages.brief: A woman stands among her collection of eighteen thousand owl items, including T-shirts and stuffed animals. In Texas, Barney Smith displays more than one thousand decorated toilet seats at his Toilet Seat Art Museum, presenting them as works of art.

pages.text: Start Your Own Collection You can start a collection of anything that interests you. People collect soap, hats, and even dirt or sand from different places. Check out the stickers on fruit in your kitchen. One woman has over ten thousand fruit stickers!
pages.brief: A person starts a collection of everyday things: soap, hats, and dirt or sand from different places. In a kitchen, fruit stickers are gathered from fruit. One woman’s collection of over ten thousand fruit stickers is shown as an example.

pages.text: Collections can be really strange. Some people collect air sickness bags. Others collect lists left behind in grocery stores! Having a collection is a fun way to spend time, meet friends, and learn new things. If you don’t already have a collection, maybe it’s time to start one.
pages.brief: Collectors show unusual collections: air sickness bags and lists left behind in grocery stores. Around them, the fun of collecting is shown as a way to spend time, meet friends, and learn new things. A newcomer looks ready to start a collection.

books.title: Rocky Mountain National Park
books.art_why: The book includes Native peoples, 1800s settlers, gold seekers, and mining towns, so historical scenes need drawings.

pages.text: Rocky Mountain National Park.
pages.brief: A wide view of a national park landscape under a clear sky. Rolling ground leads toward distant high land. No people or animals are shown. The scene is calm and open, suggesting a protected natural place.

pages.text: The Best of the Rockies Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP), in Colorado, shows off the best of the Rocky Mountains. Its air is fresh and clean. Its mountain lakes mirror high peaks above them. The park is home to mountain lions, moose, and many other wild animals. Nature lovers can enjoy the park by car or on foot.
pages.brief: A mountain lake in Colorado mirrors high peaks above it. The air looks fresh and clean. A moose stands near the water, and a mountain lion is partly visible among trees. In the distance, a car drives a road and a person walks a trail.

pages.text: Young Mountains Rocky Mountain National Park is a small part of the Rockies. They stretch 3,000 miles (4,828 km) from Canada to New Mexico. Compared to other mountain ranges, the Rockies are young. They were pushed up between one hundred million and sixty-five million years ago.
pages.brief: A long chain of rugged mountain peaks stretches across a wide landscape. The mountains look young and sharp, extending far toward the horizon. No people or animals are present. The scene suggests a huge range that goes on for thousands of miles.

pages.text: The Rockies form the Continental Divide. The mountains divide which way water flows. Water on the western side flows west into the Pacific Ocean. Water on the eastern side flows east into the Atlantic Ocean. NORTH AMERICA United States Mexico.
pages.brief: A high mountain ridge divides the land. A stream on the western side flows away to the left. A stream on the eastern side flows away to the right. The ridge rises between them under an open sky. The landscape shows how mountains separate water flow.

pages.text: From Moose to Marmots Rocky Mountain National Park has wet areas and forests of pine and aspen trees. Mountain wildflowers dot open areas with bright colors in summer. The trees stop growing at about 11,000 feet (3,353 m). This is called the tree line. Above this line, it’s too cold and rocky for trees to grow.
pages.brief: A mountainside shows forests of pine and aspen below a clear tree line. Above the line, the ground is rocky and bare, too cold for trees. In open areas below, bright wildflowers dot the ground in summer. Wet areas are visible near the forest.

pages.text: Different areas in RMNP are home to different animals. Elk and deer feed in the fields and forests. Moose wade in wet places and chomp plants there. Bobcats and a few mountain lions and black bears live in the park, too.
pages.brief: Elk and deer feed in open fields and among forest trees. A moose wades in a wet place, chomping plants. A bobcat stands near rocks, and a black bear is visible in the trees. A mountain lion is partly hidden in the background.

pages.text: Some animals live above the tree line. They include bighorn sheep and marmots, which are one of the largest members of the squirrel family. Marmots can be spotted on warm, sunny rocks. If they sense danger, they squeak. In rocky places, pika dash around. They look like big hamsters but are more like rabbits.
pages.brief: Above the tree line, a bighorn sheep stands on rocky ground. A marmot sits on a warm, sunny rock. Nearby, a pika dashes among rocks; it looks like a big hamster. The marmot has its mouth open as if about to squeak.

pages.text: About 280 kinds of birds have been seen in RMNP. Eagles and crows ride on mountain winds. One bird stays on the ground and blends in with the earth. In winter, its feathers turn white and blend in with the snow.
pages.brief: Eagles and crows ride on mountain winds high above. On the ground, a bird stays low; its brown feathers blend with the earth. In a snowy scene, the same bird's feathers turn white and blend with the snow.

pages.text: Plan a Visit One road inside the park lets drivers climb up and over the Continental Divide. This road is closed in winter, when snowdrifts can be more than 20 feet (6 m) deep.
pages.brief: A road climbs up and over a high mountain pass across the Continental Divide. Cars drive along the winding road. In winter, the road is closed, and huge snowdrifts more than 20 feet deep cover the route.

pages.text: People who love hiking can leave the sound of traffic behind. Some put their tents near mountain lakes and rushing creeks. Others follow rocky paths to climb the park’s tallest mountains. Autumn is a special time to visit the park. Aspen leaves turn bright yellow. People also come to watch and listen to elk.
pages.brief: Hikers walk away from a road, leaving traffic behind. Some pitch tents near a mountain lake and a rushing creek. Others follow a rocky path up toward tall mountains. Aspen leaves glow bright yellow in autumn, and people watch elk nearby.

pages.text: History of Rocky Mountain National Park Native peoples once lived in and traveled through the land that is now Rocky Mountain National Park. They spent summers camped in the beautiful valleys. Settlers and gold seekers began arriving in this part of the Rockies in the mid-1800s. For settlers headed west, these same mountains were hard to cross. They had to drive their wagons over the steep passes. Others built mining towns in the area. In 1915, the president signed a law creating Rocky Mountain National Park. Today, much of the land that surrounds RMNP is also protected.
