pages.brief: Native peoples camp in a beautiful valley during summer. In the mid-1800s, settlers and gold seekers arrive, driving wagons over steep mountain passes. A mining town sits nearby. A president signs a law in 1915, creating the national park.

pages.text: A Popular Park Each year, more than four million people visit RMNP from around the world. During the summer months, some parts of the park get crowded. Sometimes there are traffic jams.
pages.brief: Many visitors from around the world fill a park area in summer. Cars line up bumper to bumper in a traffic jam. People walk along paths and stand near viewpoints. The scene looks busy and crowded.

pages.text: Still, anyone who can hike a mile or two can find a way to escape the crowd.
pages.brief: A hiker walks a mile or two along a quiet trail away from a crowded area. The path leads into open nature. Few or no other people are nearby. The scene feels calm and uncrowded.

books.title: The Everglades
books.art_why: The keyword check calls for drawing, and the book includes historical Native peoples and 1800s events that cannot be photographed.

pages.text: Weird and Wonderful Have you ever heard of a gumbo-limbo? How about a skink or a stinkpot? These funny words are the names of plants and animals that live in Everglades National Park. This weird, wonderful place is unlike any other.
pages.brief: A collage-like scene in Everglades National Park showing a gumbo-limbo tree, a skink lizard, and a stinkpot turtle among plants. The odd-named plants and animals appear together, presenting the park as a weird and wonderful place unlike any other.

pages.text: More Than a Swamp Everglades National Park is in South Florida. Summers there are hot and wet, while winters are mild and dry. Water is everywhere. Many people think the Everglades is just swamps, or wetlands partly covered by water. In fact, it is home to many different communities of living things. KEY.
pages.brief: South Florida under a hot, wet summer sky, with water spread across wetlands and swamps. The scene shows different communities of living things living among the water, making clear that the Everglades is more than just a swamp.

pages.text: Native Peoples of the Everglades The Calusa were the first Native people to live in the Everglades. Most of them died from European diseases. The Seminole tribe was formed from other Native groups. In 1835, the U.S. military started a war against the Seminole people. The Seminoles went into the Everglades to escape the U.S. military. In the end, the U.S. military never overcame the Seminole people. The Everglades has different types of areas. One of these is freshwater swamps. Cypress trees grow there, and panthers, rabbits, turkey, and deer live there.
pages.brief: A historical scene of Calusa people in the Everglades, then Seminole people escaping U.S. military soldiers in 1835 into the wetlands. Nearby, a freshwater swamp shows cypress trees and a panther, rabbit, turkey, and deer living there.

pages.text: The Everglades has saltwater swamps, too. Mangrove trees, which look different from other trees, grow there. Mangroves have long roots that rise above the water. Trees with Knees Cypress trees have growths, called knees, which grow up from the tree’s roots. Part of these knees lives above water, helping bring air to the roots. The other part is below the water, helping hold the roots in place.
pages.brief: A saltwater swamp with mangrove trees whose long roots rise above the water. Beside them, a cypress tree shows knobby knees growing up from its roots, part above water bringing air and part below holding the roots in place.

pages.text: The Everglades has wet marshes where sawgrass grows. Sawgrass is a tall plant with leaves that are sharp, like a saw.
pages.brief: A wide view of a wet marsh in the Everglades filled with tall sawgrass. Its long leaves look sharp like a saw as the dense plant growth rises across the marshy ground where this tall plant grows.

pages.text: The Everglades also has woods, which are called hardwood hammocks. Tall trees that grow there shade the ground below.
pages.brief: A quiet wooded area called a hardwood hammock in the Everglades. Tall trees grow there and cast shade over the ground below, creating a shaded woods that is one of the park’s different natural places.

pages.text: A Park Is Born For many years, white settlers left the Everglades alone. Then, in 1903, things started to change. Builders wanted to put farms and homes there. They began to drain away the water, which caused the Everglades to start drying out. Other people wanted to protect the Everglades, including a writer named Marjory Stoneman Douglas. She worked hard to keep the Everglades as it was to protect the plants and animals that lived there. River of Grass In the 1940s, Marjory Stoneman Douglas wrote a book called The Everglades: River of Grass. The book was a great success. It helped save the special nature in the area.
pages.brief: A historical scene in the Everglades: builders drain water as white settlers wanted farms and homes. Nearby, writer Marjory Stoneman Douglas works to protect the plants and animals; in the 1940s her successful book about the River of Grass helped save the area’s nature.

pages.text: In 1934, the United States government set aside land for a park. It took a while, but in 1947 the area finally became a national park.
pages.brief: The United States government sets aside land in the Everglades in 1934. After time passes, in 1947, the protected area finally becomes a national park, shown as a broad natural landscape under open sky.

pages.text: Protecting the Park Today, the park is protected from builders. However, it faces other dangers. One danger is climate change causing significant differences in weather conditions. Weather shifts are hard on animals and plants, which struggle to live in new circumstances. Everglades National Park by the Numbers  1.5 million acres (607,000 ha)  Over 1 million visitors each year  More than 40 types of mammals  Over 360 types of birds  About 120 different types of trees  More than 50 unique kinds of reptiles.
pages.brief: A protected Everglades landscape under changing weather. Climate change brings significant shifts in conditions, making life hard for animals and plants that struggle in new circumstances. Nearby, many visitors and diverse mammals, birds, trees, and reptiles show the park’s richness.

pages.text: Another danger comes from animals and plants that aren’t from Florida or aren’t meant to live on their own. Some are pets that have been set free. Others include plants that grow from seeds dumped in the trash. They cause problems for the plants and animals that do belong in the Everglades. These new plants and animals may use up the things that local plants and animals need to live.
pages.brief: Non-native plants and animals cause problems in the Everglades. Some are pets set free; others are plants grown from seeds dumped in the trash. They use up things that local plants and animals need to live, crowding the Florida natives in the wetland.

pages.text: Into the Wild People come from around the world to see the Everglades. They hike on trails and paddle through swamps. They go on boat rides through marshes. A visitor kayaks through the cypress swamps.
pages.brief: People from around the world visit the Everglades. Visitors hike on trails, paddle through swamps, and take boat rides through marshes. One visitor kayaks through cypress swamps, moving into the wild among trees and water.

pages.text: Visitors take in amazing sights along the way. Beautiful birds, unusual animals, and strange plants are everywhere. Those sights remind people that Everglades National Park is a special place. The park’s natural beauty is like no other.
pages.brief: Visitors take in amazing sights along the way: beautiful birds, unusual animals, and strange plants everywhere. The natural beauty of Everglades National Park reminds people that the park is a special place like no other.

books.title: Badlands National Park
books.art_why: The book is about a real national park, its rocks, animals, and visitors.

pages.text: Badlands National Park.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor view of Badlands National Park, with open land and sky filling the scene. The park landscape is shown as a quiet place to begin a journey through its natural features, without people or animals in the foreground.

pages.text: Water and wind created the Badlands. Those forces are still hard at work there today. What’s Good About the Badlands? Tall grass waves in the wind. Bison snort in the distance. A prairie dog squeaks and disappears into its hole. Then the grass ends, and rocky peaks point toward the sky. The land is dry and brown, but sometimes the Sun shines just right. When it does, the rocks and fields of grass display surprising colors. Badlands National Park is both strange and amazing.
pages.brief: Tall grass waves in the wind while a bison stands in the distance and a prairie dog disappears into its hole. The grass ends at rocky peaks pointing toward the sky, and sunlight brings out surprising colors on the dry brown rocks and fields.

pages.text: The Park Badlands National Park (BNP) is located in South Dakota. The park helps protect wild plants and animals. About one million people visit BNP each year. Native American groups have lived there for a long time. They believe the land is special. Land of the Lakota The Lakota people have lived near Badlands National Park for more than two hundred years. They call it mako sica (mah-KOH SHEE-chah), which means “land that is bad” in their language. Scientists also use the word badlands to describe land where soft rock has been worn away by weather.
pages.brief: A broad view of the park in South Dakota, with rocky land and grass. A group of Native American people stands nearby, looking across the land they consider special; soft rock worn by weather rises around them.

pages.text: Rocks and Grass Geologists are scientists who study rocks, soil, and land to learn more about Earth’s history. BNP makes their job easier because its rocks show how the land formed. Each layer tells a story.
pages.brief: A geologist stands before layered rock formations in Badlands National Park, studying the rocks, soil, and land. The visible layers rise in steps, showing how the land formed, while the scientist looks closely at each layer to learn about Earth’s history.

pages.text: The layers contain fossil, or plants and animals that have become rock. The layers show that BNP has gone through big changes. For example, the area was once a jungle, long before humans lived there. It was also underwater for millions of years. Fossil Finds saber-toothed cat skull Many amazing fossils have been found in Badlands National Park. They include parts of giant rhinoceroses and three-toed horses. In 2010, a seven-year-old Junior Ranger named Kylie Ferguson discovered a fossil of a saber- toothed cat! Kylie Ferguson.
pages.brief: A seven-year-old Junior Ranger named Kylie Ferguson kneels on the ground in Badlands National Park, discovering a fossil of a saber-toothed cat. Nearby are parts of giant rhinoceroses and three-toed horses, and a saber-toothed cat skull rests among the layered rocks.

pages.text: Layers of Badlands National Park The Sharps Formation includes the highest peaks in the park. Its white base was made by ash from volcanoes. 25–30 million years ago The Brule Formation marks a time when the land was covered with grass and trees. 30–34 million years ago The Chadron (SHA-druhn) Formation was created when rivers left behind silt, or very small bits of rock. Alligator fossils have been found in this layer. 34–37 million years ago Yellow Mounds, which formed as a great sea disappeared, is soil made mostly of fossils. 69–75 million years ago Pierre (PEER) Shale was once black mud at the bottom of that same sea. It turned into a kind of rock called shale. Fossils of sea creatures tell the history of this layer. 69–75 million years ago Scientists study rock layers by starting at the bottom, where they usually find the oldest rocks. What story do the Badlands’ rock layers tell?
pages.brief: A scientist studies a tall stack of Badlands rock layers, starting at the bottom. The highest peaks rise above a white ash base, while lower layers show old grass and trees, river silt with alligator fossils, yellow fossil soil, and dark shale from an ancient sea.

pages.text: BNP is not all rocky; some areas are prairie, or open land covered with wild grass where few trees grow. Prairie once covered much of the United States, but most of it was turned into farm fields. Today, BNP protects an area of mixed- grass prairie.
pages.brief: An open stretch of mixed-grass prairie inside Badlands National Park, with wild grass covering the land and few trees. The prairie spreads wide under the sky, showing the kind of open grassland the park protects today, while rocky areas remain elsewhere in the park.

pages.text: Beasts of the Badlands Many animals live in the park. They must be able to survive in tough weather. Winters are very cold and windy, while summers are hot and dry. Big storms are possible anytime of year.
pages.brief: Several wild animals live in Badlands National Park under tough weather conditions. Cold wind blows across the winter landscape, while hot, dry summer ground and dark storm clouds show the hard conditions the animals must survive through the year.

pages.text: Visitors may spot bighorn sheep in rocky areas of the park. Signs tell visitors to “Beware Rattlesnakes.” These snakes use the rattles on their tails to warn away what scares them. Their bites can be dangerous, but they usually sneak away rather than bite anyone.
pages.brief: A bighorn sheep stands among rocky areas of the park while visitors keep their distance. Nearby, a rattlesnake raises its tail and shakes its rattle to warn away what scares it, then slips away rather than bite.

pages.text: Most wild animals live in the park’s grassy areas. Big brown bison feed there, and prairie dogs dig tunnels. Park rangers ask visitors to stay at least 100 yards (91 m) from wild animals. Keeping a safe distance helps protect them both.
pages.brief: In a grassy area, big brown bison feed while prairie dogs dig tunnels in the ground. A park ranger stands with visitors far back, keeping a safe distance from the wild animals so that both people and animals stay protected.

pages.text: More than two hundred kinds of birds live in the park. Hawks hunt from above, while bluebirds dart after insects. Owls make their homes underground.
pages.brief: A hawk hunts from above while bluebirds dart after insects in the park. Below them, an owl makes its home underground, showing some of the more than two hundred kinds of birds that live in Badlands National Park.

pages.text: Planning a Visit A visit to Badlands National Park is a great reason for a road trip. Visitors should wear strong shoes for hiking. They need to bring plenty of water. Many visitors enjoy BNP from inside their cars, driving along a winding road that crosses the park. There are many places to stop and take pictures. Sunrises and sunsets are the best times to take great photos.
pages.brief: Visitors drive along a winding road that crosses Badlands National Park, with places to stop and take pictures. Other visitors wear strong shoes for hiking and carry plenty of water, while sunrise or sunset light makes the landscape especially good for photographs.

pages.text: Badlands National Park is like a journey back in time. It is easy to imagine people riding on horseback through the tall grass. Rocks tell about the history of the land. Wild animals roam free, as they have for hundreds of years. The Badlands are as beautiful as they are bad.
pages.brief: People ride on horseback through tall grass in Badlands National Park, as if traveling back in time. Rocky formations rise nearby, wild animals roam free across the land, and the wide landscape shows the beauty and history of the Badlands.
